entries.8599d7caccce58ac6ff0a872243151b988858cda: <div sID="gen18183" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="50" osisID="Jer.50" sID="Jer.50"/> <div eID="gen18183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18184" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18185" type="x-p"/> In this chapter, and that which follows, we have the judgment of Babylon, which is put last of Jeremiah's prophecies against the Gentiles because it was last accomplished; and when the cup of God's fury went round ( <reference osisRef="Jer.25.17">ch.25.17</reference>) the king of Sheshach, Babylon, drank last. Babylon was employed as the rod in God's hand for the chastising of all the other nations, and now at length that rod shall be thrown into the fire. The destruction of Babylon by Cyrus was foretold, long before it came to its height, by Isaiah, and now again, when it has come to its height, by Jeremiah; for, though at this time he saw that kingdom flourishing "like a green bay-tree," yet at the same time he foresaw it withered and cut down. And as Isaiah's prophecies of the destruction of Babylon and the deliverance of Israel out of it seem designed to typify the evangelical triumphs of all believers over the powers of darkness, and the great salvation wrought out by our Lord Jesus Christ, so Jeremiah's prophecies of the same events seem designed to point at the apocalyptic triumphs of the gospel church in the latter days over the New-Testament Babylon, many passages in the Revelation being borrowed hence. The kingdom of Babylon being much larger and stronger than any of the kingdoms here prophesied against, its fall was the more considerable in itself; and, it having been more oppressive to the people of God than any of the other, the prophet is very copious upon this subject, for the comfort of the captives; and what was foretold in general often before (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.12">ch. xxv. 12</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.27.7">xxvii. 7</reference>) is here more particularly described, and with a great deal of prophetic heat as well as light. The terrible judgments God had in store for Babylon, and the glorious blessings he had in store for his people that were captives there, are intermixed and counterchanged in the prophecy of this chapter; for Babylon was destroyed to make way for the turning again of the captivity of God's people. Here is, I. The ruin of Babylon, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.1-Jer.50.3 Jer.50.9-Jer.50.16 Jer.50.21-Jer.50.32 Jer.50.35-Jer.50.46">ver. 1-3, 9-16, 21-32, and 35-46</reference>. II. The redemption of God's people, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.4-Jer.50.8 Jer.50.17-Jer.50.20 Jer.50.33 Jer.50.34">ver. 4-8, 17-20, and 33, 34</reference>. And these being set the one against the other, it is easy to say which one would choose to take one's lot with, the persecuting Babylonians, who, though now in pomp, are reserved for so great a ruin, or the persecuted Israelites, who, though now in thraldom, are reserved for so great a glory.
entries.cbf0184913819203c98ec26368da46e4cad619f6: <div eID="gen18185" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18184" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Judgment of Babylon. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 595.)</title> <div sID="gen18186" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The word that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake against Babylon <hi type="italic">and</hi> against the land of the Chaldeans by Jeremiah the prophet. <hi type="super">2</hi> Declare ye among the nations, and publish, and set up a standard; publish, <hi type="italic">and</hi> conceal not: say, Babylon is taken, Bel is confounded, Merodach is broken in pieces; her idols are confounded, her images are broken in pieces. <hi type="super">3</hi> For out of the north there cometh up a nation against her, which shall make her land desolate, and none shall dwell therein: they shall remove, they shall depart, both man and beast. <hi type="super">4</hi> In those days, and in that time, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , the children of Israel shall come, they and the children of Judah together, going and weeping: they shall go, and seek the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> their God. <hi type="super">5</hi> They shall ask the way to Zion with their faces thitherward, <hi type="italic">saying,</hi> Come, and let us join ourselves to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> in a perpetual covenant <hi type="italic">that</hi> shall not be forgotten. <hi type="super">6</hi> My people hath been lost sheep: their shepherds have caused them to go astray, they have turned them away <hi type="italic">on</hi> the mountains: they have gone from mountain to hill, they have forgotten their restingplace. <hi type="super">7</hi> All that found them have devoured them: and their adversaries said, We offend not, because they have sinned against the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , the habitation of justice, even the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , the hope of their fathers. <hi type="super">8</hi> Remove out of the midst of Babylon, and go forth out of the land of the Chaldeans, and be as the he goats before the flocks. <div eID="gen18186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18187" type="x-p"/> I. Here is a word spoken against Babylon by him whose works all agree with his word and none of whose words fall to the ground. The king of Babylon had been very kind of Jeremiah, and yet he must foretel the ruin of that kingdom; for God's prophets must not be governed by favour or affection. Whoever are our friends, if, notwithstanding, they are God's enemies, we dare not speak peace to them. 1. The destruction of Babylon is here spoken of as a thing done, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.2">v. 2</reference>. let it be published to the nations as a piece of news, true news, and great news, and news they are all concerned in; let them hang out the flag, as is usual on days of triumph, to give notice of it; let all the world take notice of it: <hi type="italic">Babylon is taken.</hi> Let God have the honour of it, let his people have the comfort of it, and therefore do not conceal it. Take care that it be known, that <hi type="italic">the Lord may be known by those judgments which he executes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.9.16">Ps. ix. 16</reference>. 2. It is spoken of as a thing done thoroughly. For, (1.) The very idols of Babylon, which the people would protect with all possible care, and from which they expected protection, shall be destroyed. Bel and Merodach were their two principal deities; they shall be <hi type="italic">confounded,</hi> and the images of them <hi type="italic">broken to pieces.</hi> (2.) The country shall be laid waste (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.3">v. 3</reference>) out <hi type="italic">of the north,</hi> from Media, which lay north of Babylon, and from Assyria, through which Cyrus made his descent upon Babylon; thence the nation shall come that shall make <hi type="italic">her land desolate.</hi> Their land was north of the countries that they destroyed, who were therefore threatened with evil from the north (<hi type="italic">Omne malum ab aquilone—Every evil comes from the north</hi>); but God will find out nations yet further north to come upon them. The pomp and power of old Rome were brought down by northern nations, the Goths and Vandals. <div eID="gen18187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18188" type="x-p"/> II. Here is a word spoken for the people of God, and for their comfort, both <hi type="italic">the children of Israel</hi> and <hi type="italic">of Judah;</hi> for many there were of the ten tribes that associated with those of the two tribes in their return out of Babylon. Now here, <div eID="gen18188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18189" type="x-p"/> 1. It is promised that they shall return to their God first and then to their own land; and the promise of their conversion and reformation is that which makes way for all the other promises, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.4-Jer.50.5">v. 4, 5</reference>. (1.) They shall <hi type="italic">lament after the Lord</hi> (as the whole house of Israel did in Samuel's time, <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.2">1 Sam. vii. 2</reference>); they shall <hi type="italic">go weeping.</hi> These tears flow not from the sorrow of the world as those when they went into captivity, but from godly sorrow; they are tears of repentance for sin, tears of joy for the goodness of God, in the dawning of the day of their deliverance, which, for aught that appears, does more towards the bringing of them to mourn for sin than all the calamities of their captivity; that prevails to <hi type="italic">lead them to repentance</hi> when the other did not prevail to drive them to it. Note, It is a good sign that God is coming towards a people in ways of mercy when they begin to be tenderly affected under his hand. (2.) They shall <hi type="italic">enquire after the Lord;</hi> they shall not sink under their sorrows, but bestir themselves to find out comfort where it is to be had: <hi type="italic">They shall go weeping to seek the Lord their God.</hi> Those that seek the Lord must <hi type="italic">seek him sorrowing,</hi> as Christ's parents sought him, <reference osisRef="Luke.2.48">Luke ii. 48</reference>. And those that sorrow must seek the Lord, and then their sorrow shall soon be turned into joy, for he will be found of those that so seek him. They shall <hi type="italic">seek the Lord as their God,</hi> and shall now have no more to do with idols. When they shall hear that the idols of Babylon are <hi type="italic">confounded and broken</hi> it will be seasonable for them to enquire after their own God and to return to him who lives for ever. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> men are deceived in false gods, that they may depend on the true God only. (3.) They shall think of returning to their own country again; they shall think of it not only as a mercy, but as a duty, because there only is the <hi type="italic">holy hill of Zion,</hi> on which once stood <hi type="italic">the house of the Lord their God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">They shall ask the way to Zion with their faces thitherward.</hi> Zion was the city of their solemnities; they often thought of it in the depth of their captivity (<reference osisRef="Ps.137.1">Ps. cxxxvii. 1</reference>); but, now that the ruin of Babylon gave them some hopes of a release, they talk of nothing else but of going back to Zion. Their hearts were upon it before, and now they <hi type="italic">set their faces thitherward.</hi> They long to be there; they set out for Zion, and resolve not to take up short of it. The journey is long and they know not the road, but they will <hi type="italic">ask the way,</hi> for they will press forward till they come to Zion; and, as they are determined not to turn back, so they are in care not to miss the way. This represents the return of poor souls to God. Heaven is the Zion they aim at as their end; on this they have set their hearts; towards this they have <hi type="italic">set their faces,</hi> and therefore they <hi type="italic">ask the way</hi> thither. They do not ask the way to heaven and set their faces towards the world; nor set their faces towards heaven and go on at a venture without asking the way. But in all true converts there are both a sincere desire to attain the end and a constant care to keep in the way; and a blessed sight it is to see people thus asking the way to heaven with their faces thitherward. (4.) They shall renew their covenant to walk with God more closely for the future: <hi type="italic">Come, and let us join ourselves to the Lord in a perpetual covenant.</hi> They had broken covenant with God, had in effect separated themselves from him, but now they resolve to <hi type="italic">join themselves</hi> to him again, by engaging themselves afresh to be his. Thus, when backsliders return, they must <hi type="italic">do their first works,</hi> must renew the covenant they first made; and it must be a <hi type="italic">perpetual covenant,</hi> that must never be broken; and, in order to that, must never be forgotten; for a due remembrance of it will be the means of a due observance of it. <div eID="gen18189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18190" type="x-p"/> 2. Their present case is lamented as very sad, and as having been long so: "<hi type="italic">My people</hi>" (for he owns them as his now that they are returning to him) "<hi type="italic">have been lost sheep</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.6">v. 6</reference>); they have <hi type="italic">gone from mountain to hill,</hi> have been hurried from place to place, and could find no pasture; <hi type="italic">they have forgotten their resting-place</hi> in their own country and cannot find their way to it." And that which aggravated their misery was, (1.) That they were <hi type="italic">led astray by their own shepherds,</hi> their own princes and priests; they turned them from their duty, and so provoked God to turn them out of their own land. It is bad with a people when their leaders cause them to err, when those that should direct them, and when those that should secure and advance their interests are the betrayers of them. (2.) That in their wanderings they lay exposed to the beasts of prey, who thought they were entitled to them, as waifs and strays that had no owner (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.7">v. 7</reference>); it is with them as with wandering sheep, <hi type="italic">all that found them have devoured them</hi> and made a prey of them; and when they did them the greatest injuries they laughed at them, telling them it was what their own prophets had many a time told them they deserved; that was far from justifying those who did them wrong, yet they bantered them with this excuse, <hi type="italic">We offend not, because they have sinned against the Lord;</hi> but they could not pretend that they had sinned against them. And see what notion they had of the Lord they had sinned against, not as the only true and living God, but only as <hi type="italic">the habitation of justice and the hope of their fathers;</hi> they had put a contempt upon the temple and upon the tradition of their ancestors, and therefore deserved to suffer these hard things. And yet it was indeed an aggravation of their sin, and justified God, though it did not justify their adversaries in what was done to them, that they had <hi type="italic">forsaken the habitation of justice</hi> and him that was <hi type="italic">the hope of their fathers.</hi> <div eID="gen18190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18191" type="x-p"/> 3. They are called upon to hasten away, as soon as ever the door of liberty was opened to them (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.8">v. 8</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Remove,</hi> not only out of the borders, but <hi type="italic">out of the midst of Babylon;</hi> though you be ever so well seated there, think not to settle there, but hasten to Zion, and <hi type="italic">be as the he-goats before the flocks;</hi> strive which shall be foremost, which shall lead in so good a work:" a he-goat is <hi type="italic">comely in going</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.30.31">Prov. xxx. 31</reference>) because he goes first. It is a graceful thing to be forward in a good work and to set others a good example.
entries.733b8464908d640c4f3612282415e853a6366d87: <div eID="gen18191" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Judgment of Babylon. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 595.)</title> <div sID="gen18192" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> For, lo, I will raise and cause to come up against Babylon an assembly of great nations from the north country: and they shall set themselves in array against her; from thence she shall be taken: their arrows <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> as of a mighty expert man; none shall return in vain. <hi type="super">10</hi> And Chaldea shall be a spoil: all that spoil her shall be satisfied, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">11</hi> Because ye were glad, because ye rejoiced, O ye destroyers of mine heritage, because ye are grown fat as the heifer at grass, and bellow as bulls; <hi type="super">12</hi> Your mother shall be sore confounded; she that bare you shall be ashamed: behold, the hindermost of the nations <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> a wilderness, a dry land, and a desert. <hi type="super">13</hi> Because of the wrath of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> it shall not be inhabited, but it shall be wholly desolate: every one that goeth by Babylon shall be astonished, and hiss at all her plagues. <hi type="super">14</hi> Put yourselves in array against Babylon round about: all ye that bend the bow, shoot at her, spare no arrows: for she hath sinned against the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">15</hi> Shout against her round about: she hath given her hand: her foundations are fallen, her walls are thrown down: for it <hi type="italic">is</hi> the vengeance of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : take vengeance upon her; as she hath done, do unto her. <hi type="super">16</hi> Cut off the sower from Babylon, and him that handleth the sickle in the time of harvest: for fear of the oppressing sword they shall turn every one to his people, and they shall flee every one to his own land. <hi type="super">17</hi> Israel <hi type="italic">is</hi> a scattered sheep; the lions have driven <hi type="italic">him</hi> away: first the king of Assyria hath devoured him; and last this Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon hath broken his bones. <hi type="super">18</hi> Therefore thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, the God of Israel; Behold, I will punish the king of Babylon and his land, as I have punished the king of Assyria. <hi type="super">19</hi> And I will bring Israel again to his habitation, and he shall feed on Carmel and Bashan, and his soul shall be satisfied upon mount Ephraim and Gilead. <hi type="super">20</hi> In those days, and in that time, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , the iniquity of Israel shall be sought for, and <hi type="italic">there shall be</hi> none; and the sins of Judah, and they shall not be found: for I will pardon them whom I reserve. <div eID="gen18192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18193" type="x-p"/> God is here by his prophet, as afterwards in his providence, proceeding in his controversy with Babylon. Observe, <div eID="gen18193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18194" type="x-p"/> I. The commission and charge given to the instruments that were to be employed in destroying Babylon. The army that is to do it is called <hi type="italic">an assembly of great nations</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.9">v. 9</reference>), the Medes and Persians, and all their allies and auxiliaries; it is called <hi type="italic">an assembly,</hi> because regularly formed by the divine will and counsel to do this execution. God will <hi type="italic">raise them up</hi> to do it, will incline them to and fit them for this service, and then he will <hi type="italic">cause them to come up,</hi> for all their motions are under his conduct and direction: he shall give the word of command, shall order them to <hi type="italic">put themselves in array against Babylon</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.14">v. 14</reference>), and then <hi type="italic">they shall put themselves in array</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.9">v. 9</reference>), for what God appoints to be done shall be done; and <hi type="italic">thence she shall be</hi> quickly <hi type="italic">taken;</hi> from their first sitting down before it they shall be still gaining ground against it till it be taken. God shall bid them <hi type="italic">shoot at her and spare no arrows</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.14">v. 14</reference>), and then <hi type="italic">their arrows shall be as of a mighty expert man,</hi> that has both skill and strength, a good eye and a good hand (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.9">v. 9</reference>); <hi type="italic">none shall return in vain.</hi> When God gives commission he will give success. Nay, they are bidden not only to <hi type="italic">shoot at her</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.14">v. 14</reference>), but to <hi type="italic">shout against her</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.15">v. 15</reference>) with a triumphant shout, as those that are already sure of victory. Those whom God directs to shoot may do so with shouting, for they are sure not to miss the mark. <div eID="gen18194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18195" type="x-p"/> II. The desolation and destruction itself that shall be brought upon Babylon. This is here set forth in a great variety of expressions. 1. The wealth of Babylon shall be a rich and easy prey to the conquerors (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">Chaldea shall be a spoil</hi> to all her destroyers, who shall enrich themselves by plundering her, and, which is strange, <hi type="italic">all that spoil her shall be satisfied;</hi> they shall have so much that even they themselves shall say that they have enough. 2. The country of Babylon shall be depopulated and lie uninhabited: <hi type="italic">It shall be wholly desolate</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.13">v. 13</reference>) to such a degree that <hi type="italic">every one who goes by</hi> shall triumph in her fall, and, instead of condoling with them, shall <hi type="italic">hiss at all her plagues,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.50.13">v. 13</reference>. 3. Their ancestors shall be ashamed of their cowardice, in fleeing from the first onset (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.12">v. 12</reference>), or, <hi type="italic">Your mother,</hi> Babylon itself, the mother-city, <hi type="italic">shall be confounded,</hi> when she sees herself deserted by those that should have been her guards. Thus the former ages of Christians may justly be confounded and ashamed to see how unlike them the latter ages are, and how wretchedly they have degenerated; and no sin brings a surer and sorer ruin upon persons, or people, than apostasy. 4. The great admirers of Babylon shall see it rendered very despicable: the last of kingdoms, the very tail of the nations, <hi type="italic">shall it be, a wilderness, a dry land, a desert,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.50.11">v. 11</reference>. The country that was populous shall be dispeopled, that was enriched with a fertile soil shall become barren. 5. The great city, the head of it, shall be quite ruined. <hi type="italic">Her foundations have fallen,</hi> and therefore <hi type="italic">her walls are thrown down;</hi> for how can the walls stand when divine vengeance is at the door and shakes the very foundations? It is the vengeance of the Lord, which nothing can contend with either in law or battle. 6. There shall not be left in Babylon so much as <hi type="italic">the poor of the land, for vine-dressers and husbandmen,</hi> as there was in Israel (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">The sower shall be cut off from Babylon, and he that handles the sickle;</hi> the country shall be so emptied of people that there shall be none to till the ground and gather in the fruits of it. Harvest shall come, and there shall be no reapers; seed-time shall come, but there shall be no sower; God will do his part, but there shall be no men to do theirs. 7. All their auxiliary forces, which they have hired into their service, shall desert them, as mercenary men often do upon the approach of danger (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">For fear of the oppressing sword they shall turn every one to his people.</hi> This was threatened before concerning Egypt, <reference osisRef="Jer.46.16">ch. xlvi. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen18195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18196" type="x-p"/> III. The procuring provoking cause of this destruction. It comes from God's displeasure; it is <hi type="italic">because of the wrath of the Lord</hi> that Babylon <hi type="italic">shall be wholly desolate</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.13">v. 13</reference>), and his wrath is righteous, for (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.14">v. 14</reference>) <hi type="italic">she hath sinned against the Lord,</hi> therefore <hi type="italic">spare no arrows.</hi> Note, It is sin that makes men a mark for the arrows of God's judgments. An abundance of idolatry and immorality was to be found in Babylon, yet those are not mentioned as the reason of God's displeasure against them, but the injuries they had done to the people of God, from a principle of enmity to them as his people. They have been <hi type="italic">the destroyers of God's heritage</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.11">v. 11</reference>); herein indeed God made use of them for the necessary correction of his people, and yet it is laid to their charge as a heinous crime, because they designed nothing but their utter destruction. 1. What they did against Jerusalem they did with pleasure (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">You were glad, you rejoice.</hi> God does not afflict his people willingly, and therefore takes it very ill if the instruments he employs afflict them willingly. When Titus Vespasian destroyed Jerusalem he wept over it, but these Chaldeans triumphed over it. 2. The spoils of Jerusalem they made use of to feed their own luxury: "<hi type="italic">You have grown fat as the heifer at grass, and bellow as bulls;</hi> your having conquered Jerusalem has made you very wanton and proud, easy to yourselves and formidable to all about you, and therefore you must <hi type="italic">be a spoil.</hi>" Those that have thus swallowed down riches must vomit them up again. Therefore they have <hi type="italic">given their hand</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.15">v. 15</reference>); they have surrendered themselves to the conqueror, have tamely yielded so that now you may <hi type="italic">take vengeance on her,</hi> now you may make reprisals and <hi type="italic">do unto her as she hath done.</hi> 3. They aimed at nothing less than the utter ruin of God's Israel: <hi type="italic">Israel is a scattered sheep,</hi> as before (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.6">v. 6</reference>), that is not only barked at and worried by dogs, but even lions, the most potent adversaries, have roared upon him and <hi type="italic">driven him away,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.50.17">v. 17</reference>. One king of Assyria carried the ten tribes quite away and devoured them; another invaded Judah, and plundered and impoverished it, tore the fleece and flesh of this poor sheep; and now at last this Nebuchadnezzar, that is the terror and plague of all his neighbours, has taken advantage of the low condition to which he is reduced, and he has fallen upon him and <hi type="italic">broken his bones,</hi> has quite ruined him, and therefore the king of Babylon must be punished as the king of Assyria was, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.18">v. 18</reference>. Note, Those who pursue and prosecute the sins of their predecessors must expect to be pursued and prosecuted by their plagues; if they do as they did, let them fare as they fared. <div eID="gen18196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18197" type="x-p"/> IV. The mercy promised to the Israel of God, which shall not only accompany, but accrue from, the destruction of Babylon. 1. God will return their captivity; they shall be released out of their bondage, and <hi type="italic">brought again to their own habitation</hi> as sheep that were scattered to their own fold <reference osisRef="Jer.50.19">v. 19</reference>. They still retained a title to the land of Canaan; it is their habitation still. The discontinuance of their possession was not the destruction of their right. But now they shall recover the enjoyment of it again. 2. He will restore their prosperity; they shall not only live, but live comfortably, in their own land again; they shall <hi type="italic">feed upon Carmel and Bashan,</hi> the richest and most fruitful parts of the country. These sheep shall be gathered from the deserts to which they were dispersed, and put again into good pasture, which their soul shall be satisfied with though they shall come hungry to it, having been so long stinted, and straitened, and kept short, yet they shall find enough to satiate them and shall have hearts to be satiated with it. They <hi type="italic">enquired the way to Zion</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.5">v. 5</reference>), where God was to be served and worshipped. This was what they chiefly aimed at in their return; but God will not only bring them thither, but bring them also to Carmel and Bashan, where they shall abundantly feed themselves. Note, Those that return to God and their duty shall find true satisfaction of soul in so doing; and those that <hi type="italic">seek first the kingdom of God and the righteousness thereof,</hi> that aim to make their habitation in Zion, the holy hill, shall have <hi type="italic">other things added to them,</hi> even all the comforts of <hi type="italic">Ephraim and Gilead,</hi> the fruitful hills. 3. God will pardon their iniquity; this is the root of all the rest (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">In those days the iniquity of Israel shall be sought for, and there shall be none.</hi> Not only the punishments of their iniquity shall be taken off, but the offence which it gave to God shall be forgotten, and he will be reconciled to them. Their sin shall be before him as if it had never been; it shall be blotted out as a cloud, crossed out as a debt, shall be cast behind his back; nay, it shall be cast into the depth of the sea, shall be no longer sealed up among God's treasures, nor in any danger of appearing again or rising up against them. This denotes how fully God forgives sin; he <hi type="italic">remembers it no more.</hi> Note, Deliverances out of trouble are then comforts indeed when they are the fruits of the forgiveness of sin, <reference osisRef="Isa.38.17">Isa. xxxviii. 17</reference>. Judah and Israel were so fully forgiven when they were brought back out of Babylon that they are said to have <hi type="italic">received of the Lord's hand double for all their sins,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.40.1">Isa. xl. 1</reference>. This may include also a thorough reformation of their hearts and lives, as well as a full remission of their sins. If any seek for idols or any idolatrous customs among them, after their return, <hi type="italic">there shall be none,</hi> they <hi type="italic">shall not find them;</hi> their dross shall be purely purged away, and by that it shall appear that their guilt is so; <hi type="italic">for I will pardon those whom I reserve; I will be propitious to them</hi> (so the word is) and that must be through him who is the great propitiation. Note, Those whose sins God pardons he reserves for something very great; for <hi type="italic">whom he justifies them he</hi> glorifies.
entries.8449018a9bc4ed4669f81ca4be3ce21229914db7: <div eID="gen18197" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Judgment of Babylon. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 595.)</title> <div sID="gen18198" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> Go up against the land of Merathaim, <hi type="italic">even</hi> against it, and against the inhabitants of Pekod: waste and utterly destroy after them, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and do according to all that I have commanded thee. <hi type="super">22</hi> A sound of battle <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the land, and of great destruction. <hi type="super">23</hi> How is the hammer of the whole earth cut asunder and broken! how is Babylon become a desolation among the nations! <hi type="super">24</hi> I have laid a snare for thee, and thou art also taken, O Babylon, and thou wast not aware: thou art found, and also caught, because thou hast striven against the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">25</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath opened his armoury, and hath brought forth the weapons of his indignation: for this <hi type="italic">is</hi> the work of the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> of hosts in the land of the Chaldeans. <hi type="super">26</hi> Come against her from the utmost border, open her storehouses: cast her up as heaps, and destroy her utterly: let nothing of her be left. <hi type="super">27</hi> Slay all her bullocks; let them go down to the slaughter: woe unto them! for their day is come, the time of their visitation. <hi type="super">28</hi> The voice of them that flee and escape out of the land of Babylon, to declare in Zion the vengeance of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God, the vengeance of his temple. <hi type="super">29</hi> Call together the archers against Babylon: all ye that bend the bow, camp against it round about; let none thereof escape: recompense her according to her work; according to all that she hath done, do unto her: for she hath been proud against the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , against the Holy One of Israel. <hi type="super">30</hi> Therefore shall her young men fall in the streets, and all her men of war shall be cut off in that day, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">31</hi> Behold, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> against thee, <hi type="italic">O thou</hi> most proud, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> of hosts: for thy day is come, the time <hi type="italic">that</hi> I will visit thee. <hi type="super">32</hi> And the most proud shall stumble and fall, and none shall raise him up: and I will kindle a fire in his cities, and it shall devour all round about him. <div eID="gen18198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18199" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. The forces are mustered and commissioned to destroy Babylon, and every thing is got ready for a descent upon that potent kingdom: <hi type="italic">Go up against</hi> that <hi type="italic">land</hi> by <hi type="italic">Merathaim,</hi> the country of the Mardi, that lay part in Assyria and part in Armenia; and go among <hi type="italic">the inhabitants of Pekod,</hi> another country (mentioned <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.23">Ezek. xxiii. 23</reference>) which Cyrus took in his way to Babylon. The forces of Cyrus are called to go up against Babylon (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.21">v. 21</reference>), to <hi type="italic">come against her from the utmost border.</hi> Let all come together, for there will be both work and pay enough for them all, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.26">v. 26</reference>. Distance of place must not be their hindrance from engaging in this work. <hi type="italic">The archers</hi> particularly must be <hi type="italic">called together against Babylon,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.50.29">v. 29</reference>. Thus <hi type="italic">the Lord hath opened his armoury</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.25">v. 25</reference>), <hi type="italic">his treasury</hi> (so the word is), <hi type="italic">and hath brought forth the weapons of his indignation,</hi> as great princes fetch out of their magazines and stores all necessary provisions for their armies when they undertake any great expedition. Media and Persia are now God's armoury; thence he fetches the weapons of his wrath, Cyrus and his great officers and armies, whom he will make use of for the destruction of Babylon. Note, Great men are but instruments which the great God makes use of to serve his own purposes. He has variety of instruments, has them at command, has armouries ready to be opened according as the occasion is. <hi type="italic">This is the work of the Lord God of hosts.</hi> Note, When God has work to do he will make it appear that he is <hi type="italic">God of hosts,</hi> and will not want instruments to do it with. 2. Instructions are given them what to do. In general, <hi type="italic">Do according to all that I have commanded thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.50.21">v. 21</reference>. It was said of Cyrus (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.28">Isa. xliv. 28</reference>), <hi type="italic">He shall perform all my pleasure,</hi> in his expedition against Babylon. They must <hi type="italic">waste and utterly destroy after them;</hi> when they have destroyed once they must go over them again, or destroy their posterity that should come after them. They must <hi type="italic">open her store-houses</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.26">v. 26</reference>), rifle her treasures, and turn her artillery against herself. They must <hi type="italic">cast her up as heaps;</hi> let all the wealth and pomp of Babylon be shovelled up in a heap of ruins and rubbish. <hi type="italic">Tread her down as heaps</hi> (so the margin reads it) <hi type="italic">and destroy her utterly.</hi> See how little account the great God makes of those things which men so much value and value themselves so much upon. Their princes and great men, who are fat and bulky, shall fall by the sword, not as men of war in the field of battle, which we call a bed of honour, but as beasts by the butcher's hand (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.27">v. 27</reference>): <hi type="italic">Slay all her bullocks,</hi> all her mighty men; <hi type="italic">let them go down</hi> sottishly and insensibly, as an ox <hi type="italic">to the slaughter. Woe unto them!</hi> their case is the more sad for the little sense they have of it. <hi type="italic">Their day has come</hi> to fall, <hi type="italic">the time</hi> when they must be reckoned with, and they are not aware of it. 3. Assurances are given them of success. Let them do what God commands, and they shall accomplish what he threatens. A <hi type="italic">great destruction</hi> shall be made, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.21">v. 21</reference>. <hi type="italic">Babylon</hi> shall <hi type="italic">become a desolation</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.23">v. 23</reference>); <hi type="italic">her young men and all her men of war shall be cut off in that day</hi> which should have been her defence, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.30">v. 30</reference>. God is <hi type="italic">against</hi> her (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.31">v. 31</reference>); he has <hi type="italic">laid a snare for</hi> her (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.24">v. 24</reference>); he has formed this enterprise against her, that she should be surprised as a bird taken in a snare. Cyrus shall no doubt prevail, for he fights under God. God <hi type="italic">will kindle a fire</hi> in the cities of Babylon (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.32">v. 32</reference>); and who can stand before him when he is angry, or quench the fire that he has kindled? 4. Reasons are given for these severe dealings with Babylon. Those that are employed in this war may, if they please, know the grounds of it, and be satisfied in the justice of it, which it is fit all should be that are called to such work. (1.) Babylon has been very troublesome, vexatious, and injurious, to all its neighbours; it has been <hi type="italic">the hammer of the whole earth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.23">v. 23</reference>), beating, beating down, and beating to pieces, all the nations far and near. It has done so long enough; it is time now that it be <hi type="italic">cut asunder and broken.</hi> Note, He that is the god of nations will sooner or later assert the injured rights of nations against those that unjustly and violently invade them. The God of the whole earth will break <hi type="italic">the hammer of the whole earth.</hi> (2.) Babylon has bidden defiance to God himself: <hi type="italic">Thou has striven against the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.24">v. 24</reference>), <hi type="italic">hast joined issue with him</hi> (so the word signifies) as in law or battle, hast openly opposed him, set up rivals with him, raised rebellion against him; therefore <hi type="italic">thou art</hi> now <hi type="italic">found, and caught,</hi> as in a snare. Note, Those that strive against the Lord will soon find themselves over-matched. (3.) Babylon ruined Jerusalem, the holy city, and the holy house there, and must now be called to an account for that. This is the manifesto published in Zion, in the day of Babylon's visitation; it is <hi type="italic">the vengeance of the Lord our God, the vengeance of his temple,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.50.28">v. 28</reference>. The burning of the temple, and the carrying away of its vessels, were articles in the charge against Babylon on which greater stress was laid than upon its being <hi type="italic">the hammer of the whole earth;</hi> for Zion was <hi type="italic">the joy</hi> and glory <hi type="italic">of the whole earth.</hi> Note, Whatever wrong is done to God's church (his temple in the world) it will certainly be reckoned for; and no vengeance will be sorer nor heavier than <hi type="italic">the vengeance of the temple.</hi> (4.) Babylon has been very haughty and insolent, and therefore must have a fall; for it is the glory of God to <hi type="italic">look upon those that are proud and to abase them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.40.11">Job xl. 11</reference>. <hi type="italic">I am against thee, O thou most proud!</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.50.31">v. 31</reference> and again <reference osisRef="Jer.50.31">v. 31</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thou pride</hi> (so the word is), as proud as pride itself. Note, the pride of men's hearts sets God against them and ripens them apace for ruin; for God <hi type="italic">resists the proud</hi> and will bring them down. <hi type="italic">The most proud shall stumble and fall;</hi> they shall fall not so much by others' thrusting them down as by their own stumbling; for they hold their heads so high that they never look under their feet, to choose their way and avoid stumbling-blocks, but walk at all adventures. Babylon's pride must unavoidably be her ruin; for <hi type="italic">she has been proud against the Lord, against the Holy One of Israel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.29">v. 29</reference>), has insulted him in insulting over his people; she has made him her enemy, and therefore, when she has <hi type="italic">fallen, none shall raise her up,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.50.31">v. 31</reference>. Who can help those up whom God will throw down?
entries.743087391fe6d97aa4ab7813cbed8352775ff737: <div eID="gen18199" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Judgment of Babylon. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 595.)</title> <div sID="gen18200" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">33</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts; The children of Israel and the children of Judah <hi type="italic">were</hi> oppressed together: and all that took them captives held them fast; they refused to let them go. <hi type="super">34</hi> Their Redeemer <hi type="italic">is</hi> strong; the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts <hi type="italic">is</hi> his name: he shall thoroughly plead their cause, that he may give rest to the land, and disquiet the inhabitants of Babylon. <hi type="super">35</hi> A sword <hi type="italic">is</hi> upon the Chaldeans, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and upon the inhabitants of Babylon, and upon her princes, and upon her wise <hi type="italic">men.</hi> <hi type="super">36</hi> A sword <hi type="italic">is</hi> upon the liars; and they shall dote: a sword <hi type="italic">is</hi> upon her mighty men; and they shall be dismayed. <hi type="super">37</hi> A sword <hi type="italic">is</hi> upon their horses, and upon their chariots, and upon all the mingled people that <hi type="italic">are</hi> in the midst of her; and they shall become as women: a sword <hi type="italic">is</hi> upon her treasures; and they shall be robbed. <hi type="super">38</hi> A drought <hi type="italic">is</hi> upon her waters; and they shall be dried up: for it <hi type="italic">is</hi> the land of graven images, and they are mad upon <hi type="italic">their</hi> idols. <hi type="super">39</hi> Therefore the wild beasts of the desert with the wild beasts of the islands shall dwell <hi type="italic">there,</hi> and the owls shall dwell therein: and it shall be no more inhabited for ever; neither shall it be dwelt in from generation to generation. <hi type="super">40</hi> As God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah and the neighbour <hi type="italic">cities</hi> thereof, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; <hi type="italic">so</hi> shall no man abide there, neither shall any son of man dwell therein. <hi type="super">41</hi> Behold, a people shall come from the north, and a great nation, and many kings shall be raised up from the coasts of the earth. <hi type="super">42</hi> They shall hold the bow and the lance: they <hi type="italic">are</hi> cruel, and will not shew mercy: their voice shall roar like the sea, and they shall ride upon horses, <hi type="italic">every one</hi> put in array, like a man to the battle, against thee, O daughter of Babylon. <hi type="super">43</hi> The king of Babylon hath heard the report of them, and his hands waxed feeble: anguish took hold of him, <hi type="italic">and</hi> pangs as of a woman in travail. <hi type="super">44</hi> Behold, he shall come up like a lion from the swelling of Jordan unto the habitation of the strong: but I will make them suddenly run away from her: and who <hi type="italic">is</hi> a chosen <hi type="italic">man, that</hi> I may appoint over her? for who <hi type="italic">is</hi> like me? and who will appoint me the time? and who <hi type="italic">is</hi> that shepherd that will stand before me? <hi type="super">45</hi> Therefore hear ye the counsel of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , that he hath taken against Babylon; and his purposes, that he hath purposed against the land of the Chaldeans: Surely the least of the flock shall draw them out: surely he shall make <hi type="italic">their</hi> habitation desolate with them. <hi type="super">46</hi> At the noise of the taking of Babylon the earth is moved, and the cry is heard among the nations. <div eID="gen18200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18201" type="x-p"/> We have in these verses, <div eID="gen18201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18202" type="x-p"/> I. Israel's sufferings, and their deliverance out of those sufferings. God takes notice of the bondage of his people in Babylon, as he did of their bondage in Egypt; he has <hi type="italic">surely seen</hi> it, and has <hi type="italic">heard their cry. Israel and Judah were oppressed together,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.50.33">v. 33</reference>. Those that remained of the captives of the ten tribes, upon the uniting of the kingdoms of Assyria and Chaldea, seem to have come and mingled with those of the two tribes, and to have mingled tears with them, so that they were <hi type="italic">oppressed together.</hi> They were humble suppliants for their liberty, and that was all; they could not attempt any thing towards it, for <hi type="italic">all that took them captives held them fast,</hi> and were much too hard for them. But this is their comfort in distress, that, though they are weak, <hi type="italic">their Redeemer is strong</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.34">v. 34</reference>), <hi type="italic">their Avenger</hi> (so the word signifies), he that has a right to them, and will claim his right and make good his claim. He is stronger than their enemies that hold them fast; he can overpower all the force that is against them, and put strength into his own people though they are very weak. <hi type="italic">The Lord of hosts is his name,</hi> and he will answer to his name, and make it to appear that he is what his people call him, and will be that to them for which they depend upon him. Note, It is the unspeakable comfort of the people of God that, though they have hosts against them, they have <hi type="italic">the Lord of hosts</hi> for them and <hi type="italic">he shall thoroughly plead their cause,</hi> pleading he shall plead it, plead it with jealousy, plead it effectually, plead it and carry it, <hi type="italic">that he may give rest to the land,</hi> and to his people's land, rest from all their enemies round about. This is applicable to all believers, who complain of the dominion of sin and corruption, and of their own weakness and manifold infirmities. Let them know that <hi type="italic">their Redeemer is strong;</hi> he is able to keep what they commit to him, and he will plead their cause. Sin shall not have dominion over them; he will <hi type="italic">make them free,</hi> and they shall be <hi type="italic">free indeed;</hi> he will give them <hi type="italic">rest,</hi> that <hi type="italic">rest which remains for the people of God.</hi> <div eID="gen18202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18203" type="x-p"/> II. Babylon's sin, and their punishment for that sin. <div eID="gen18203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18204" type="x-p"/> 1. The sins they are here charged with are idolatry and persecution. (1.) They oppressed the people of God; they <hi type="italic">held them fast,</hi> and would not <hi type="italic">let them go.</hi> They <hi type="italic">opened not the house of his prisoners,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.14.17">Isa. xiv. 17</reference>. This was God's quarrel with them, as of old with Pharaoh; it cost him dear, and yet they would not take warning. <hi type="italic">The inhabitants of Babylon</hi> must be <hi type="italic">disquieted</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.34">v. 34</reference>) because they have disquieted God's people, whose honour and comfort he is jealous for, and therefore will <hi type="italic">recompense tribulation to those that trouble them,</hi> as well as <hi type="italic">rest to those that are troubled,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.1.6-2Thess.1.7">2 Thess. i. 6, 7</reference>. (2.) They wronged God himself, and robbed him, giving that glory to others which is due to him alone; for (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.38">v. 38</reference>) <hi type="italic">it is the land of graven images.</hi> All parts of the country abounded with idols, and they were mad upon them, were in love with them and doted on them, cared not what cost and pains they were at in the worship of them, were unwearied in paying their respects to them; and in all this they were wretchedly infatuated and acted like men out of their wits; they were carried on in their idolatry without reason or discretion, like men in a perfect fury. The word here used for idols properly signifies <hi type="italic">terrors—Enim,</hi> the name given to giants that were formidable, because they made the images of their gods to look frightful, to strike a terror upon fools and children. Their idols were scarecrows, yet they doted on them. Babylon was <hi type="italic">the mother of harlots</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.17.5">Rev. xvii. 5</reference>), the source of idolatry. Note, It is the maddest thing in the world to make a god of any creature; and those who are proud against the Lord, the true God, are justly given up to strong delusions, to be mad upon idols that cannot profit. But this madness is wickedness, for which sinners will be certainly and severely reckoned with. <div eID="gen18204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18205" type="x-p"/> 2. The judgments of God upon them for these sins are such as will quite lay them waste and ruin them. <div eID="gen18205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18206" type="x-p"/> (1.) All that should be their defence and support shall be cut off by the sword. The Chaldeans had long been God's sword, wherewith he had done execution upon the sinful nations round about: but now, they being as bad as any of them, or worse, <hi type="italic">a sword</hi> is brought upon them, even <hi type="italic">upon the inhabitants of Babylon</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.35">v. 35</reference>), a sword of war; and, as it is in God's hand, sent and directed by him, it is a sword of justice. It shall be, [1.] <hi type="italic">Upon their princes;</hi> they shall fall by it, and their dignity, wealth, and power, shall not secure them. [2.] <hi type="italic">Upon their wise men,</hi> their philosophers, their statesmen, and privy-counsellors; their learning and policy shall neither secure them nor stand the public in any stead. [3.] <hi type="italic">Upon</hi> their soothsayers and astrologers, here called <hi type="italic">the liars</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.36">v. 36</reference>), for they cheated with their prognostications of peace and prosperity; the sword upon them shall make them dote, so that they shall talk like fools, and be as men that have lost all their wits. Note, God has a sword that can reach the soul and affect the mind, and bring men under spiritual plagues. [4.] <hi type="italic">Upon their mighty men.</hi> A sword shall be upon their spirits; if they are not slain, yet <hi type="italic">they shall be dismayed,</hi> and shall be no longer <hi type="italic">mighty men;</hi> for what stead will their hands stand them in when their hearts fail them? [5.] Upon their militia (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.37">v. 37</reference>): <hi type="italic">The sword shall be upon their horses and chariots;</hi> the invaders shall make themselves masters of all their warlike stores, shall seize their horses and chariots for themselves, or destroy them. The troops of other nations that were in their service shall be quite disheartened: <hi type="italic">The mingled people shall become as</hi> weak and timorous as <hi type="italic">women.</hi> [6.] Upon their exchequer: The <hi type="italic">sword</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">upon her treasures,</hi> which are the sinews of war, <hi type="italic">and they shall be robbed,</hi> and made use of by the enemy against them. See what universal destruction the sword makes when it comes with commission. <div eID="gen18206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18207" type="x-p"/> (2.) The country shall be made desolate (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.38">v. 38</reference>): <hi type="italic">The waters shall be dried up,</hi> the water that secures the city. Cyrus drew the river Euphrates into so many channels as made it passable for his army, so that they got with ease to the walls of Babylon, which, if was thought, that river had rendered inaccessible. "The water likewise that made the country fruitful shall <hi type="italic">be dried up,</hi> so that it shall be turned into barrenness, and shall be no more inhabited by the children of men, but by <hi type="italic">the wild beasts of the desert,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Jer.50.39">v. 39</reference>. This was foretold concerning Babylon, <reference osisRef="Isa.13.19-Isa.13.21">Isa. xiii. 19-21</reference>. It shall become like <hi type="italic">Sodom and Gomorrah,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.50.40">v. 40</reference>. The same was foretold concerning Edom, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.18">ch. xlix. 18</reference>. As the Chaldeans had laid Edom waste, so they shall themselves be laid waste. <div eID="gen18207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18208" type="x-p"/> (3.) The king and kingdom shall be put into the utmost confusion and consternation by the enemies' invading them, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.41-Jer.50.43">v. 41-43</reference>. All the expressions here used to denote the formidable power of the invaders, the terrors wherewith they should array themselves, and the great fright which both court and country should be put into thereby, we met with before (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.22-Jer.6.24">ch. vi. 22-24</reference>) concerning the Chaldeans' invading the land of Judah. The battle which is there said to be <hi type="italic">against thee, O daughter of Zion!</hi> is here said to be <hi type="italic">against thee, O daughter of Babylon!</hi> to intimate that they should be paid in their own coin. God can find out such as shall be for terror and destruction to those that are for terror and destruction to others; and those who have dealt cruelly, and have shown no mercy, may expect to be cruelly dealt with, and to find no mercy. Only there is one difference between these passages; there it is said, <hi type="italic">We have heard the fame thereof and our hands wax feeble;</hi> here it is said, <hi type="italic">The king of Babylon has heard the report and his hands waxed feeble,</hi> which intimates that that proud and daring prince shall, in the day of his distress, be as weak and dispirited as the meanest Israelites were in the day of their distress. <div eID="gen18208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18209" type="x-p"/> (4.) That they shall be as much hurt as frightened, for the invader shall <hi type="italic">come up like a lion</hi> to tear and destroy (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.44">v. 44</reference>) and shall make them and their <hi type="italic">habitation desolate</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.45">v. 45</reference>), and the desolation shall be so astonishing that all the nations about shall be terrified by it, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.46">v. 46</reference>. These three verses we had before (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.19-Jer.49.21">ch. xlix. 19-21</reference>) in the prophecy of the destruction of Edom, which was accomplished by the Chaldeans, and they are here repeated, <hi type="italic">mutatis mutandis—with a few necessary alterations,</hi> in the prophecy of the destruction of Babylon, which was to be accomplished upon the Chaldeans, to show that though the distributions of Providence may appear unequal for a time its retributions will be equal at last; when thou shalt make <hi type="italic">an end to spoil thou shalt be spoiled,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.33.1">Isa. xxxiii. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.13.10">Rev. xiii. 10</reference>.  <chapter eID="Jer.50"/> <div eID="gen18209" type="x-p"/>

entries.d57cf2df8e559fadd8378ba9842168942540727e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10668"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 50</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Jer.50.1-Jer.50.46">Jr 50:1-46</reference>. Babylon's Coming Downfall; Israel's Redemption.</title> <div sID="gen19086" type="x-p"/> After the predictions of judgment to be inflicted on other nations by Babylon, follows this one against Babylon itself, the longest prophecy, consisting of one hundred verses. The date of utterance was the fourth year of Zedekiah, when Seraiah, to whom it was committed, was sent to Babylon (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.59">Jr 51:59</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.60">60</reference>). The repetitions in it make it likely that it consists of prophecies uttered at different times, now collected by Jeremiah to console the Jews in exile and to vindicate God's ways by exhibiting the final doom of Babylon, the enemy of the people of God, after her long prosperity. The style, imagery, and dialogues prove its genuineness in opposition to those who deny this. It shows his faithfulness; though under obligation to the king of Babylon, he owed a higher one to God, who directed him to prophesy against Babylon.<div eID="gen19086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19087" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10668"/>1. Compare Is 45:1-47:15. But as the time of fulfilment drew nearer, the prophecies are now proportionally more distinct than then. <div eID="gen19087" type="x-p"/>
entries.6473ef2150fc3116c7f7127d846a5d1ca1108f50: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10669"/><div sID="gen19088" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10669"/><hi type="bold">2. Declare ... among ... nations--</hi>who would rejoice at the fall of Babylon their oppressor.<div eID="gen19088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19089" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">standard--</hi>to indicate the place of meeting to the nations where they were to hear the good news of Babylon's fall [Rosenmuller]; or, the signal to summon the nations together against Babylon (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.12">Jr 51:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.27">27</reference>), [Maurer].<div eID="gen19089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19090" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Bel--</hi>the tutelary god of Babylon; the same idol as the Phoenician Baal, that is, lord, the sun (<reference osisRef="Isa.46.1">Is 46:1</reference>).<div eID="gen19090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19091" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">confounded--</hi>because unable to defend the city under their protection.<div eID="gen19091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19092" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Merodach--</hi>another Babylonian idol; meaning in Syria "little lord"; from which Merodach-baladan took his name. <div eID="gen19092" type="x-p"/>
entries.2045fbc7090cc8fa5e3e104304aa71b287ad837f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10670"/><div sID="gen19093" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10670"/><hi type="bold">3. a nation--</hi>the Medes, north of Babylon (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.48">Jr 51:48</reference>). The devastation of Babylon here foretold includes not only that by Cyrus, but also that more utter one by Darius, who took Babylon by artifice when it had revolted from Persia, and mercilessly slaughtered the inhabitants, hanging four thousand of the nobles; also the final desertion of Babylon, owing to Seleucia having been built close by under Seleucus Nicanor. <div eID="gen19093" type="x-p"/>
entries.d91892260d7c26cb459a25a05bb0815f6853f189: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10671"/><div sID="gen19094" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10671"/>4. Fulfilled only in part when some few of the ten tribes of "Israel" joined Judah in a "covenant" with God, at the restoration of Judah to its land (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.38">Ne 9:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.10.29">10:29</reference>). The full event is yet to come (<reference osisRef="Jer.31.9">Jr 31:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.1.11">Ho 1:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.12.10">Zec 12:10</reference>).<div eID="gen19094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19095" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">weeping--</hi>with joy at their restoration beyond all hope; and with sorrow at the remembrance of their sins and sufferings (<reference osisRef="Ezra.3.12">Ezr 3:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.13">13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.126.5">Psa 126:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.126.6">6</reference>).<div eID="gen19095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19096" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seek ... Lord--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Hos.3.5">Ho 3:5</reference>). <div eID="gen19096" type="x-p"/>
entries.ddc455d2bae9c27c423a5c571e2059bc64ed5d66: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10672"/><div sID="gen19097" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10672"/><hi type="bold">5. thitherward--</hi>rather, "hitherward," Jeremiah's prophetical standpoint being at Zion. "Faces hitherward" implies their steadfastness of purpose not to be turned aside by any difficulties on the way.<div eID="gen19097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19098" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">perpetual covenant--</hi>in contrast to the old covenant "which they brake" (<reference osisRef="Jer.31.31">Jr 31:31</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="Jer.32.40">Jr 32:40</reference>). They shall return to their God first, then to their own land. <div eID="gen19098" type="x-p"/>
entries.5a2534a79c0b4b4ae8da2c7386da7e77a41cff9c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10673"/><div sID="gen19099" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10673"/>6. (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.6">Is 53:6</reference>).<div eID="gen19099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19100" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">on the mountains--</hi>whereon they sacrificed to idols (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.20">Jr 2:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.6">3:6</reference>, 23).<div eID="gen19100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19101" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">resting-place--</hi>for the "sheep," continuing the image; Jehovah is the resting-place of His sheep (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.28">Mt 11:28</reference>). They rest in His "bosom" (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.11">Is 40:11</reference>). Also His temple at Zion, their "rest," because it is His (<reference osisRef="Ps.132.8">Psa 132:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.132.14">14</reference>). <div eID="gen19101" type="x-p"/>
entries.c5918a58281270117a6ddaf98251d8ae9fd9ae2a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10674"/><div sID="gen19102" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10674"/><hi type="bold">7. devoured--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.79.7">Psa 79:7</reference>). "Found them" implies that they were exposed to the attacks of those whoever happened to meet them.<div eID="gen19102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19103" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">adversaries said--</hi>for instance, Nebuzara-dan (<reference osisRef="Jer.40.2">Jr 40:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.40.3">3</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Zech.11.5">Zec 11:5</reference>). The Gentiles acknowledged some supreme divinity. The Jews' guilt was so palpable that they were condemned even in the judgment of heathens. Some knowledge of God's peculiar relation to Judea reached its heathen invaders from the prophets (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.3">Jr 2:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.9.16">Da 9:16</reference>); hence the strong language they use of Jehovah here, not as worshippers of Him themselves, but as believing Him to be the tutelary God of Judah ("the hope of their fathers," <reference osisRef="Ps.22.4">Psa 22:4</reference>; they do not say our hope), as each country was thought to have its local god, whose power extended no farther.<div eID="gen19103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19104" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">habitation--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.90.1">Psa 90:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.91.1">91:1</reference>). Alluding to the tabernacle, or, as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.14">Eze 34:14</reference>, "fold," which carries out the image in <reference osisRef="Jer.50.6">Jr 50:6</reference>, "resting-place" of the "sheep." But it can only mean "habitation" (<reference osisRef="Jer.31.23">Jr 31:23</reference>), which confirms English Version here.<div eID="gen19104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19105" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hope of their fathers--</hi>This especially condemned the Jews that their apostasy was from that God whose faithfulness their fathers had experienced. At the same time these "adversaries" unconsciously use language which corrects their own notions. The covenant with the Jews' "fathers" is not utterly set aside by their sin, as their adversaries thought; there is still "a habitation" or refuge for them with the God of their fathers. <div eID="gen19105" type="x-p"/>
entries.5b9d9fc06bc9f7622b669ab0bcc77ce78d248cfe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10675"/><div sID="gen19106" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10675"/>8. (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.6">Jr 51:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.45">45</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.48.20">Is 48:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.2.6">Zec 2:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.18.4">Re 18:4</reference>). Immediately avail yourselves of the opportunity of escape.<div eID="gen19106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19107" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be as ... he-goats before ... flocks--</hi>Let each try to be foremost in returning, animating the weak, as he-goats lead the flock; such were the companions of Ezra (<reference osisRef="Ezra.1.5">Ezr 1:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.6">6</reference>). <div eID="gen19107" type="x-p"/>
entries.278d28428a9027ef2f55b032047a1f7fd518c6cd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10676"/><div sID="gen19108" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10676"/><hi type="bold">9. from thence--</hi>that is, from the north country.<div eID="gen19108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19109" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">expert--</hi>literally, "prosperous." Besides "might," "expertness" is needed, that an arrow may do execution. The Margin has a different Hebrew reading; "destroying," literally, "bereaving, childless-making" (<reference osisRef="Jer.15.7">Jr 15:7</reference>). The Septuagint and Syriac support English Version.<div eID="gen19109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19110" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">In vain--</hi>without killing him at whom it was aimed (<reference osisRef="2Sam.1.22">2Sa 1:22</reference>). <div eID="gen19110" type="x-p"/>
entries.fa60e069b93aa3db918cb8d150b895b68316d325: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10677"/><div sID="gen19111" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10677"/>11. (<reference osisRef="Isa.47.6">Is 47:6</reference>).<div eID="gen19111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19112" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">grown fat--</hi>and so, skip wantonly.<div eID="gen19112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19113" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">at grass--</hi>fat and frisky. But there is a disagreement of gender in Hebrew reading thus. The Keri is better: "a heifer threshing"; the strongest were used for threshing, and as the law did not allow their mouth to be muzzled in threshing (<reference osisRef="Deut.25.4">De 25:4</reference>), they waxed wanton with eating.<div eID="gen19113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19114" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bellow as bulls--</hi>rather, "neigh as steeds," literally, "strong ones," a poetical expression for steeds (see on <reference osisRef="Jer.8.16">Jr 8:16</reference>) [Maurer]. <div eID="gen19114" type="x-p"/>
entries.edad278f4ef7c52877553bd29acc16b51b327c8d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10678"/><div sID="gen19115" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10678"/><hi type="bold">12. Your mother--</hi>Babylon, the metropolis of the empire.<div eID="gen19115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19116" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hindermost--</hi>marvellous change, that Babylon, once the queen of the world, should be now the hindermost of nations, and at last, becoming "a desert," cease to be a nation! <div eID="gen19116" type="x-p"/>
entries.51bbb556cd3ecf14766cafbaa368a0bfba21e097: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10679"/><div sID="gen19117" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10679"/>13. (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.20">Is 13:20</reference>). <div eID="gen19117" type="x-p"/>
entries.63c2c2aaeaf76d80f8ad0246563e1d8709bed2dc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10680"/><div sID="gen19118" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10680"/>14. Summons to the Median army to attack Babylon.<div eID="gen19118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19119" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">against the Lord--</hi>By oppressing His people, their cause is His cause. Also by profaning His sacred vessels (<reference osisRef="Dan.5.2">Da 5:2</reference>). <div eID="gen19119" type="x-p"/>
entries.350ae0a9d006467ea92bebef492c8ce5e9a66089: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10681"/><div sID="gen19120" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10681"/><hi type="bold">15. Shout--</hi>Inspirit one another to the onset with the battle cry.<div eID="gen19120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19121" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">given ... hand--</hi>an idiom for, "submitted to" the conquerors (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.24">1Ch 29:24</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Lam.5.6">La 5:6</reference>).<div eID="gen19121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19122" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as she hath done, do unto her--</hi>just retribution in kind. She had destroyed many, so must she be destroyed (<reference osisRef="Ps.137.8">Psa 137:8</reference>). So as to spiritual Babylon (<reference osisRef="Rev.18.6">Re 18:6</reference>). This is right because "it is the vengeance of the Lord"; but this will not justify private revenge in kind (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.44">Mt 5:44</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.12.19-Rom.12.21">Ro 12:19-21</reference>); even the Old Testament law forbade this, though breathing a sterner spirit than the New Testament (<reference osisRef="Exod.23.4">Ex 23:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.23.5">5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.25.21">Pr 25:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.25.22">22</reference>). <div eID="gen19122" type="x-p"/>
entries.e5f20ed77bfcedeea02e852c9785d127358950dc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10682"/><div sID="gen19123" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10682"/>16. Babylon had the extent rather of a nation than of a city. Therefore grain was grown within the city wall sufficient to last for a long siege [Aristotle, Politics, 3.2; Pliny, 18.17]. Conquerors usually spare agriculturists, but in this case all alike were to be "cut off."<div eID="gen19123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19124" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for fear of ... oppressing sword--</hi>because of the sword of the oppressor.<div eID="gen19124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19125" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">every one to his people--</hi>from which they had been removed to Babylon from all quarters by the Chaldean conquerors (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.9">Jr 51:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.13.14">Is 13:14</reference>). <div eID="gen19125" type="x-p"/>
entries.ce9b624103c0a59b1404a093e2a3f68d4b42b792: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10683"/><div sID="gen19126" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10683"/><hi type="bold">17. lions--</hi>hostile kings (<reference osisRef="Jer.4.7">Jr 4:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.19">49:19</reference>).<div eID="gen19126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19127" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Assyria--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.6">2Ki 17:6</reference>, Shalmaneser; <reference osisRef="Ezra.4.2">Ezr 4:2</reference>, Esar-haddon).<div eID="gen19127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19128" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Nebuchadnezzar--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.10">2Ki 24:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.14">14</reference>). <div eID="gen19128" type="x-p"/>
entries.213f3ea2a5321f8fe8a52765bb1d68140e43c02e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10684"/><div sID="gen19129" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10684"/><hi type="bold">18. punish ... king of Babylon--</hi>Nabonidus, or Labynitus.<div eID="gen19129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19130" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as ... punished ... Assyrian--</hi>Sennacherib and other kings [Grotius] (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.37">2Ki 19:37</reference>). <div eID="gen19130" type="x-p"/>
entries.a5613d30f0c191990a6c28d37cf3bb8a5fa14a52: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10685"/><div sID="gen19131" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10685"/>19. (<reference osisRef="Isa.65.10">Is 65:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.13">Eze 34:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.14">14</reference>). <div eID="gen19131" type="x-p"/>
entries.a63208f75f9b8c936dde5f0f5a86ac25f1d8802a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10686"/><div sID="gen19132" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10686"/>20. The specification of "Israel," as well as Judah, shows the reference is to times yet to come.<div eID="gen19132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19133" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">iniquity ... none--</hi>not merely idolatry, which ceased among the Jews ever since the Babylonian captivity, but chiefly their rejection of Messiah. As in a cancelled debt, it shall be as if it had never been; God, for Christ's sake, shall treat them as innocent (<reference osisRef="Jer.31.34">Jr 31:34</reference>). Without cleansing away of sin, remission of punishment would be neither to the honor of God nor to the highest interests of the elect.<div eID="gen19133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19134" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whom I reserve--</hi>the elect "remnant" (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.9">Is 1:9</reference>). The "residue" (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.2">Zec 14:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.13.8">13:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.13.9">9</reference>). <div eID="gen19134" type="x-p"/>
entries.e70d6695a156033a36d061cbadbef16ec9a49530: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10687"/><div sID="gen19135" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10687"/><hi type="bold">21. Merathaim--</hi>a symbolical name for Babylon, the doubly rebellious, namely, against God. Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.50.24">Jr 50:24</reference>, "thou hast striven against the Lord"; and <reference osisRef="Jer.50.29">Jr 50:29</reference>, "proud against the Lord." The "doubly" refers to: first, the Assyrian's oppression of Israel; next, the kindred Chaldean's oppression of Judah (compare Jr 50:17-20, 33; especially <reference osisRef="Jer.50.18">Jr 50:18</reference>).<div eID="gen19135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19136" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Pekod--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.23">Eze 23:23</reference>); a chief province of Assyria, in which Nineveh, now overthrown, once lay. But, as in Merathaim, the allusion is to the meaning of Pekod, namely, "visitation"; the inhabitants whose time of deserved visitation in punishment is come; not, however, without reference to the now Babylonian province, Pekod. The visitation on Babylon was a following up of that on Assyria.<div eID="gen19136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19137" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">after them--</hi>even their posterity, and all that is still left of Babylon, until the very name is extinct [Grotius]. Devastate the city, after its inhabitants have deserted it.<div eID="gen19137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19138" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all ... I ... commanded--</hi>by Isaiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.1">Is 13:1</reference>, &c.). <div eID="gen19138" type="x-p"/>
entries.b1d072fe0226779609da09eb15136e0930e82c66: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10688"/><div sID="gen19139" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10688"/><hi type="bold">23. hammer--</hi>that is, Babylon, so called because of its ponderous destructive power; just as "Martel," that is, "a little hammer," was the surname of a king of the Franks (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.6">Is 14:6</reference>). <div eID="gen19139" type="x-p"/>
entries.a87dd00ba9243f09aef91ed9389a43b519708cdf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10689"/><div sID="gen19140" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10689"/><hi type="bold">24. I--</hi>Thou hast to do with God, not merely with men.<div eID="gen19140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19141" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">taken ... not aware--</hi>Herodotus relates that one half of the city was taken before those in the other half were "aware" of it. Cyrus turned the waters of the Euphrates where it was defended into a different channel, and so entered the city by the dried-up channel at night, by the upper and lower gates (<reference osisRef="Dan.5.30">Da 5:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.31">31</reference>). <div eID="gen19141" type="x-p"/>
entries.c1a1075bf3718a83e2cf7bb801f1b5a25965167b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10690"/><div sID="gen19142" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10690"/><hi type="bold">25. weapons of his indignation--</hi>the Medes and Persians (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.5">Is 13:5</reference>). <div eID="gen19142" type="x-p"/>
entries.d41d917460534dca971db2733f6bc4f869d7bb8a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10691"/><div sID="gen19143" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10691"/><hi type="bold">26. from the utmost border--</hi>namely, of the earth.
