Or, from all sides [Ludovicus De Dieu].<div eID="gen19143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19144" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">storehouses--</hi>or, "her houses filled with men and goods" [Michaelis]. When Cyrus took it, the provisions found there were enough to have lasted for many years.<div eID="gen19144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19145" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as heaps--</hi>make of the once glorious city heaps of ruins. Vast mounds of rubbish now mark the site of ancient Babylon. "Tread her as heaps of corn which are wont to be trodden down in the threshing-floor" [Grotius]. <div eID="gen19145" type="x-p"/>
entries.c7b5d7c0775d5006005ef0cc5850fd4013dbc09e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10692"/><div sID="gen19146" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10692"/><hi type="bold">27. bullocks--</hi>that is, princes and strong warriors (<reference osisRef="Jer.46.21">Jr 46:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.22.12">Psa 22:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.34.7">Is 34:7</reference>).<div eID="gen19146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19147" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">go down to ... slaughter--</hi>The slaughterhouses lay low beside the river; therefore it is said, "go down"; appropriate to Babylon on the Euphrates, the avenue through which the slaughterers entered the city. <div eID="gen19147" type="x-p"/>
entries.430d182e7ead89dc7a4cc1a0c25a4ad029d6a24b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10693"/><div sID="gen19148" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10693"/><hi type="bold">28. declare in Zion ... temple--</hi>Some Jews "fleeing" from Babylon at its fall shall tell in Judea how God avenged the cause of Zion and her temple that had been profaned (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.13">Jr 52:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.1.2">Da 1:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.2">5:2</reference>). <div eID="gen19148" type="x-p"/>
entries.82bf2f252f1294028ae358c37e4fbedf4f566064: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10694"/><div sID="gen19149" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10694"/><hi type="bold">29. archers--</hi>literally, "very many and powerful"; hence the Hebrew word is used of archers (<reference osisRef="Job.16.13">Job 16:13</reference>) from the multitude and force of their arrows.<div eID="gen19149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19150" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">according to all that she hath done--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Jer.50.15">Jr 50:15</reference>).<div eID="gen19150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19151" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">proud against the Lord--</hi>not merely cruel towards men (<reference osisRef="Isa.47.10">Is 47:10</reference>). <div eID="gen19151" type="x-p"/>
entries.d118b96651d1673042825c50e05254fdf060f0bc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10695"/><div sID="gen19152" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10695"/>30. (See on <reference osisRef="Jer.49.26">Jr 49:26</reference>).<div eID="gen19152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19153" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the streets--</hi>The Babylonians were so discouraged by having lost some battles that they retired within their walls and would not again meet Cyrus in the field. <div eID="gen19153" type="x-p"/>
entries.293530e156f01f1b4ab6db36b953acefff4fa856: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10696"/><div sID="gen19154" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10696"/><hi type="bold">31. most proud--</hi>literally, "pride"; that is, man of pride; the king of Babylon.<div eID="gen19154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19155" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">visit--</hi>punish (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.27">Jr 50:27</reference>). <div eID="gen19155" type="x-p"/>
entries.037e118bac995334135138de470bc989df2e6a22: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10697"/><div sID="gen19156" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10697"/><hi type="bold">33. Israel and ... Judah were oppressed--</hi>He anticipates an objection, in order to answer it: Ye have been, no doubt, "oppressed," therefore ye despair of deliverance; but, remember your "Redeemer is strong," and therefore can and will deliver you. <div eID="gen19156" type="x-p"/>
entries.3c06705b9d102637ace189cb4ebe401226f21c37: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10698"/><div sID="gen19157" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10698"/><hi type="bold">34. strong--</hi>as opposed to the power of Israel's oppressor (<reference osisRef="Rev.18.8">Re 18:8</reference>).<div eID="gen19157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19158" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">plead ... cause--</hi>as their advocate. Image from a court of justice; appropriate as God delivers His people not by mere might, but by righteousness. His plea against Satan and all their enemies is His own everlasting love, reconciling mercy and justice in the Redeemer's work and person (<reference osisRef="Mic.7.9">Mi 7:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.3.1-Zech.3.5">Zec 3:1-5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.2.1">1Jo 2:1</reference>).<div eID="gen19158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19159" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">give rest ... disquiet--</hi>There is a play on the similarity of sounds in the two Hebrew verbs to express more vividly the contrast: "that He may give quiet to the land of Judah (heretofore disquieted by Babylon); but disquiet to the inhabitants of Babylon" (heretofore quietly secure) (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.6-Isa.14.8">Is 14:6-8</reference>). <div eID="gen19159" type="x-p"/>
entries.a21372ad6efc7209b540f3fedb96648d68c5aca0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10699"/><div sID="gen19160" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10699"/>35-37. The repetition of "A sword" in the beginning of each verse, by the figure anaphora, heightens the effect; the reiterated judgment is universal; the same sad stroke of the sword is upon each and all connected with guilty Babylon.<div eID="gen19160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19161" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wise men--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.47.13">Is 47:13</reference>). Babylon boasted that it was the peculiar seat of wisdom and wise men, especially in astronomy and astrology. <div eID="gen19161" type="x-p"/>
entries.48bc99723de93327306183227db30d41b5bd9a04: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10702"/><div sID="gen19164" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10702"/><hi type="bold">38. drought--</hi>Altering the pointing, this verse will begin as the three previous verses, "A sword." However, all the pointed manuscripts read, "A drought," as English Version. Cyrus turned off the waters of the Euphrates into a new channel and so marched through the dried-up bed into the city (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.32">Jr 51:32</reference>). Babylonia once was famed for its corn, which often yielded from one to two hundredfold [Herodotus]. This was due to its network of water-courses from the Euphrates for irrigation, traces of which [Layard] are seen still on all sides, but dry and barren (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.27">Is 44:27</reference>).<div eID="gen19164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19165" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their idols--</hi>literally, "terrors." They are mad after idols that are more calculated to frighten than to attract (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.44">Jr 51:44</reference>, 47, 52; <reference osisRef="Dan.3.1">Da 3:1</reference>). Mere bugbears with which to frighten children. <div eID="gen19165" type="x-p"/>
entries.a01dfad83dbd38905b5ce950034ec01e0b37cece: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10703"/><div sID="gen19166" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10703"/><hi type="bold">39. wild beasts of the desert--</hi>wild cats, remarkable for their howl [Bochart].<div eID="gen19166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19167" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wild beasts of the islands--</hi>jackals (See on <reference osisRef="Isa.13.21">Is 13:21</reference>).<div eID="gen19167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19168" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">owls--</hi>rather, "female ostriches"; they delight in solitary places. Literally, "daughters of crying." Compare as to spiritual Babylon, <reference osisRef="Rev.18.2">Re 18:2</reference>.<div eID="gen19168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19169" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no more inhabited for ever--</hi>The accumulation of phrases is to express the final and utter extinction of Babylon; fulfilled not immediately, but by degrees; Cyrus took away its supremacy. Darius Hystaspes deprived it, when it had rebelled, of its fortifications. Seleucus Nicanor removed its citizens and wealth to Seleucia, which he founded in the neighborhood; and the Parthians removed all that was left to Ctesiphon. Nothing but its walls was left under the Roman emperor Adrian. <div eID="gen19169" type="x-p"/>
entries.86d3a7df9437970d5c1a345f07a94049ef926f78: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10704"/><div sID="gen19170" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10704"/>40. (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.19">Is 13:19</reference>). Repeated from <reference osisRef="Jer.49.18">Jr 49:18</reference>. <div eID="gen19170" type="x-p"/>
entries.2ee257d2559328f8743a11aa769180ccaecc181c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10705"/><div sID="gen19171" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10705"/>41-43. (Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.6.22-Jer.6.24">Jr 6:22-24</reference>). The very language used to describe the calamities which Babylon inflicted on Zion is that here employed to describe Babylon's own calamity inflicted by the Medes. Retribution in kind.<div eID="gen19171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19172" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">kinds--</hi>the allies and satraps of the various provinces of the Medo-Persian empire: Armenia, Hyrcania, Lydia, &c.<div eID="gen19172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19173" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">coasts--</hi>the remote parts. <div eID="gen19173" type="x-p"/>
entries.03fe18ea7f42016893e4818590fe188439a7de8d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10708"/><div sID="gen19177" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10708"/>44-46. Repeated mainly from <reference osisRef="Jer.49.19-Jer.49.21">Jr 49:19-21</reference>. The identity of God's principle in His dealing with Edom, and in that with Babylon, is implied by the similarity of language as to both. <div eID="gen19177" type="x-p"/>

entries.14aec6fb7b85ffaf5a369ce73cd77237bab606fb: <div eID="gen30676" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen30677" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen30678" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen30678" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen30677" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen30679" type="x-p"/> This and the following chapter contain a prophecy relating to the fall of Babylon, interspersed with several predictions relative to the restoration of Israel and Judah, who were to survive their oppressors, and, on their repentance, to be pardoned and brought to their own land. This chapter opens with a prediction of the complete destruction of all the Babylonish idols, and the utter desolation of Chaldea, through the instrumentality of a great northern nation, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.1-Jer.50.3">Jer 50:1-3</reference>. Israel and Judah shall be reinstated in the land of their forefathers after the total overthrow of the great Babylonish empire, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.4">Jer 50:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.5">Jer 50:5</reference>. Very oppressive and cruel bondage of the Jewish people during the captivity, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.6">Jer 50:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.7">Jer 50:7</reference>. The people of God are commanded to remove speedily from Babylon, because an assembly of great nations are coming out of the north to desolate the whole land, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.8-Jer.50.10">Jer 50:8-10</reference>. Babylon, the hammer of the whole earth, the great desolator of nations, shall itself become a desolation on account of its intolerable pride, and because of the iron yoke it has rejoiced to put upon a people whom a mysterious Providence had placed under its domination, vv. 11-34. The judgments which shall fall upon Chaldea, a country addicted to the grossest idolatry, and to every species of superstition, shall be most awful and general, as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.35-Jer.50.40">Jer 50:35-40</reference>. Character of the people appointed to execute the Divine judgments upon the oppressors of Israel, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.41-Jer.50.45">Jer 50:41-45</reference>. Great sensation among the nations at the very terrible and sudden fall of Babylon, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.46">Jer 50:46</reference>. <div eID="gen30679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30680" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen30680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30681" type="x-p"/> The Word that the Lord Spake Against Babylon - This is also a new head of discourse. <div eID="gen30681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30682" type="x-p"/> The prophecy contained in this and the following chapter was sent to the captives in Babylon in the fourth year of the reign of Zedekiah. They are very important; they predict the total destruction of the Babylonish empire, and the return of the Jews from their captivity. These chapters were probably composed, with several additions, out of the book that was then sent by Jeremiah to the captives by the hand of Seraiah. See <reference osisRef="Jer.51.59-Jer.51.64">Jer 51:59-64</reference>.
entries.80b29c715c0686777381093c67f88f999a8ec3df: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen30682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30683" type="x-p"/> Declare ye among the nations - God's determination relative to this empire. <div eID="gen30683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30684" type="x-p"/> Set up a standard - Show the people where they are to assemble. <div eID="gen30684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30685" type="x-p"/> Say, Babylon is taken - It is a thing so firmly determined, that it is as good as already done. <div eID="gen30685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30686" type="x-p"/> Bel - The tutelar deity of Babylon is confounded, because it cannot save its own city. <div eID="gen30686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30687" type="x-p"/> Merodach - Another of their idols, is broken to pieces; it was not able to save itself, much less the whole empire. <div eID="gen30687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30688" type="x-p"/> Her idols are confounded - It is a reproach to have acknowledged them. <div eID="gen30688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30689" type="x-p"/> Her images - Great and small, golden and wooden, are broken to pieces; even the form of them no longer appears.
entries.7844c8321af4725aa496d2eed607761bf9bfea44: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen30689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30690" type="x-p"/> Out of the north there cometh up a nation - The Medes, who formed the chief part of the army of Cyrus, lay to the north or north-east of Babylon. <div eID="gen30690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30691" type="x-p"/> Shall make her land desolate - This war, and the consequent taking of the city, began those disasters that brought Babylon in process of time to complete desolation; so that now it is not known where it stood, the whole country being a total solitude.
entries.2a00b59ee19ed893ced9fe0227dfbd4fcb884bd6: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen30691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30692" type="x-p"/> In those days, and in that time - In the times in which Babylon shall be opposed by the Medes and Persians, both Israel and Judah, seeing the commencement of the fulfilling of the prophecies, shall begin to seek the Lord with much prayer, and broken and contrite hearts. When the decree of Cyrus comes, they shall be ready to set off for their own country, deploring their offenses, yet rejoicing in the mercy of God which has given them this reviving in their bondage.
entries.c305493112a736b974115fcb5b3a24f3492c4dea: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen30692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30693" type="x-p"/> Let us join ourselves to the Lord in a perpetual covenant - All our former covenants have been broken; let us now make one that shall last for ever. He shall be the Lord Our God, and We will no more worship idols. This covenant they have kept to the present day; whatever their present moral and spiritual state may be, they are no idolaters, in the gross sense of the term. <div eID="gen30693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30694" type="x-p"/> The description that is here given of the state of this people, their feelings and their conduct, finely exhibit the state of real penitents, who are fervently seeking the salvation of their souls. <div eID="gen30694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30695" type="x-p"/> 1. In those days when Jesus Christ is manifested in the flesh; and in that time, when through him is preached the remission of sins, and the people who hear are pricked in their conscience. <div eID="gen30695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30696" type="x-p"/> 2. The children of Israel and the children of Judah together. - No distinctions being then felt or attended to; for all feel themselves sinners, who have come short of the glory of God. Even national distinctions and religious differences, which bind men fastest, and hold them longest, are absorbed in the deep and overpowering concern they feel for their eternal interests. <div eID="gen30696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30697" type="x-p"/> 3. Going and weeping shall they go. - Religious sorrow does not preclude activity and diligence. While they are weeping for their sins, they are going on in the path of duty, seeking the Lord while he may be found, and calling upon him while he is near. <div eID="gen30697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30698" type="x-p"/> 4. They shall ask the way to Zion. - Real penitents are the most inquisitive of all mortals; but their inquiries are limited to one object, they ask the way to Zion. What shall we do to be saved? How shall we shun the perdition of ungodly men, etc. <div eID="gen30698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30699" type="x-p"/> 5. With their faces thitherward. - They have turned from sin, and turned To God. They have left the paths of the destroyer, and their hearts are towards God, and the remembrance of his name. Thus they are profiting by that light which has convinced them of sin, righteousness, and judgment. <div eID="gen30699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30700" type="x-p"/> 6. Come, and let us join ourselves to the Lord. - Religion is a social principle, and begets a social feeling in the soul. No man who feels his own sore, and the plague of his heart, wishes to venture alone in the way to heaven. He feels he wants counsel, support, comfort and the company of those who will watch over him in love. Like David, the true penitent is a companion of all those who fear the Lord. These heavenly feelings come from one and the same Spirit, and lead to the same end; hence they say, - <div eID="gen30700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30701" type="x-p"/> 7. Let us join ourselves to the Lord in a perpetual covenant. It is said, that to be undecided, is to be decided. They who are not determined to go to heaven, will never reach it. If the heart be not laid under obligation, it will do nothing. "I hope I am in earnest; I trust I shall be in earnest about the salvation of my soul, it is very proper I should be so;" and such like, show an irresolute soul. Such persons are ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth. <div eID="gen30701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30702" type="x-p"/> Let us therefore bind ourselves. We have trifled too long; been indecisive too long; have halted too long between two opinions. We know now that Jehovah is God; let us, therefore, enter into a covenant with him. Let this covenant be a perpetual one: let us not make it for a day, for any particular time, but for ever; and let it never be broken. Let our part be kept inviolable: we Are and Will Be thy people; and God's part will never fail, I Am and Will Be your God. <div eID="gen30702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30703" type="x-p"/> The covenant requires a sacrifice. - Hence ברית berith signifies both. Christ crucified is the great covenant sacrifice. By him God becomes united to us, and through him we become united to God.
entries.34e8b9243b0f83ade6f5a88af0dfa3b2a0260b70: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen30703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30704" type="x-p"/> My people hath been lost sheep - He pities them; for their pastors, kings, and prophets have caused them to err. <div eID="gen30704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30705" type="x-p"/> They have gone from mountain to hill - In all high places they have practiced idolatry.
entries.032c74b3992d743e29b0d1aa65eaf942f31a665d: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen30705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30706" type="x-p"/> Their adversaries said, We offend not - God has abandoned them; we are only fulfilling his designs in plaguing them.
entries.8d9a080756444762e8f93825b3a7be56be837bb2: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen30706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30707" type="x-p"/> Remove out of the midst of Babylon - The sentence of destruction is gone out against it; prepare for your flight, that ye be not overwhelmed in its ruin. <div eID="gen30707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30708" type="x-p"/> Be as the he-goats before the flocks - Who always run to the head of the flock, giving the example for others to follow. This may be addressed to the elders and persons of authority among the people.
entries.b648bca886a0887a8a99aafeb47e39385ab8658c: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen30708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30709" type="x-p"/> An assembly of great nations - The army of Cyrus was composed of Medes, Persians, Armenians, Caducians, Sacae, etc. Though all these did not come from the north; yet they were arranged under the Medes, who did come from the north, in reference to Babylon. <div eID="gen30709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30710" type="x-p"/> Their arrows - They are such expert archers, that they shall never miss their mark.
entries.d3ee577637170165e4b87369ecd61ceeba65ce19: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen30710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30711" type="x-p"/> Chaldea shall be a spoil - She has been a spoiler, and she shall be spoiled. They had destroyed Judea, God's heritage; and now God shall cause her to be destroyed.
entries.55b86b68e0c7959d9d220ac19ba78bbc13f6c2fe: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen30711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30712" type="x-p"/> As the heifer at grass - Ye were wanton in the desolations ye brought upon Judea.
entries.b6ffc40e2531e03511d41b18e8136afc6720e037: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen30712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30713" type="x-p"/> Your mother - Speaking to the Chaldeans: Babylon, the metropolis, or mother city, shall be a wilderness, a dry land, a desert, neither fit for man nor beast.
entries.7711fcbfa670037b8bf23d0526382b6045f8cfbc: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen30713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30714" type="x-p"/> Shout against her round about - Encompass her with lines and with troops; let none go in with relief, none come out to escape from her ruin.
entries.67d46c72863b54df014e470f4d7c7e2eb9f9d430: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen30714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30715" type="x-p"/> Cut off the sower - Destroy the gardens and the fields, that there may be neither fruits nor tillage.
entries.e50cfda90e35c37fda7d25901aac1d2212a570d8: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen30715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30716" type="x-p"/> Israel - All the descendants of Jacob have been harassed and spoiled, first by the Assyrians, and afterwards by the Chaldeans. They acted towards them as a lion to a sheep which he has caught; first he devours all the flesh, next he breaks all the bones to extract the marrow.
entries.b9f50b1e2a4d6adb3252676face8d7748314f398: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen30716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30717" type="x-p"/> As I have punished the king of Assyria - The Assyrians were overthrown by the Medes and the Chaldeans. The king is here taken for all their kings, generals, etc., Tiglath-pileser, Shalmaneser, Sennacherib, Esar-haddon, etc. To them succeeded the Chaldean or Babylonish kings. Nebuchadnezzar came against Judea several times; and at last took the city and burnt it, profaned and demolished the temple, wasted the land, and carried the princes and people into captivity.
entries.22b6e1717098de59dd8dc6e551293f1204cd9958: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen30717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30718" type="x-p"/> I will bring Israel again - This seems to refer wholly to the ten tribes; for Carmel, Bashan, Mount Ephraim, and Gilead, were in their territories.
entries.ac5e274c7dc818ecbdf6021d9e3cafa92b4cea1f: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen30718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30719" type="x-p"/> In those days and in that time - This phrase appears to take in the whole of an epoch, from its commencement to its end. See <reference osisRef="Jer.50.4">Jer 50:4</reference>. <div eID="gen30719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30720" type="x-p"/> I will pardon them - So as to deliver them from their captivity, and exact no more punishment from them whom I reserve, namely, the remnant left in the Babylonish captivity.
entries.e4342fd4536916d95aa256bf3dcac9ce632a58f0: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen30720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30721" type="x-p"/> Go up against the land of Merathaim - and against the inhabitants of Pekod - No such places as these are to be found any where else; and it is not likely that places are at all meant. The ancient Versions agree in rendering the first as an appellative, and the last as a verb, except the Chaldee, which has Pekod as a proper name. Dr. Blayney translates: - "Against the land of bitternesses, go up: <div eID="gen30721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30722" type="x-p"/> Upon it, and upon its inhabitants, visit, O sword!" <div eID="gen30722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30723" type="x-p"/> Dr. Dahler renders thus: - "March against the country doubly rebellious, <div eID="gen30723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30724" type="x-p"/> And against its inhabitants worthy of punishment." <div eID="gen30724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30725" type="x-p"/> The latter of these two versions I take to be the most literal. The words are addressed to the Medes and Persians; and the country is Chaldea, doubly rebellious by its idolatry and its insufferable pride. In these two, it was exceeded by no other land.
entries.2d6bd731bd9ed4515f0a177dff9e12a2c110dce9: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen30725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30726" type="x-p"/> The hammer of the whole earth - Nebuchadnezzar dashed to pieces the nations against whom he warred. He was the scourge of the Lord.
entries.1a76e0e48e7dc126f2dd3c1acb4ab538bda2f187: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen30726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30727" type="x-p"/> I have laid a snare for thee - It was not by storm that Cyrus took the city. The Euphrates ran through it; he dug a channel for the river in another direction, to divert its stream; he waited for that time in which the inhabitants had delivered themselves up to debauchery: in the dead of the night he turned off the stream, and he and his army entered by the old channel, now void of its waters. This was the snare of which the prophet here speaks. See Nerodotus, lib. i., c. 191.
entries.5ddaba2d4de7e46b2338b2710182672741ae873a: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen30727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30728" type="x-p"/> Open her store-houses - At the time that Cyrus took the city, it was full of provisions and treasures of all kinds; the walls had suffered no injury; and when the inhabitants heard that the enemy was within, they thought they must have arisen out of the earth in the center of the city!
entries.acb81e9ac30a36fac11cd85ef51f7b80b5166c65: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen30728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30729" type="x-p"/> Slay all her bullocks - Princes, magistrates, etc., etc.
entries.78c508f1c74742dc83c15938f060a4ded99fc731: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen30729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30730" type="x-p"/> Declare in Zion the vengeance of the Lord - Zion was desolated by Babylon; tell Zion that God hath desolated the desolator. <div eID="gen30730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30731" type="x-p"/> The vengeance of his temple - Which Nebuchadnezzar had pillaged, profaned, and demolished, transporting its sacred vessels to Babylon, and putting them in the temple of his god Bel.
entries.2b7ca675a6d0d6fca73c43bdb71fcc838bbc2906: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen30731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30732" type="x-p"/> Call together the archers - The preceding verses are the prediction: here, God calls the Medes and Persians to fulfill it.
entries.80bc04cc61a5f408f7119cd00292e4edb01a4a67: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen30732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30733" type="x-p"/> O thou most proud - זדון zadon. Pride in the abstract; proudest of all people.
entries.408e79039cd6559fb5cc62452f2e01e22b96fb9b: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen30733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30734" type="x-p"/> And the most proud - זדון zadon, as before. Here pride is personified and addressed, as if possessing a being and rational powers.
entries.881790c286ea58dbc444b239f11f065aecde616e: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen30734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30735" type="x-p"/> Their Redeemer is strong - And it was not that he wanted power, and that Nebuchadnezzar had much, that Jerusalem was taken; but because the people had sinned, and would not return; and therefore national sins called for national punishments. These have taken place; and now the Lord of hosts shows them that the power of the Chaldeans is mere weakness against his might.
entries.6edcaa33b1d65ed600e3fc33784ec3091c6a10c4: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen30735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30736" type="x-p"/> A sword - War and its calamities, or any grievous plague; and so in the following verses.
entries.9588d0e311c2755e4522975c9c8722b62e711f8f: <hi type="bold">Verse 38</hi> <div eID="gen30736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30737" type="x-p"/> A drought is upon her waters - May not this refer to the draining of the channel of the Euphrates, by which the army of Cyrus entered the city. See on <reference osisRef="Jer.50.24">Jer 50:24</reference> (note). The original is, however, חרב chereb, a sword, as in the preceding verses, which signifies war, or any calamity by which the thing on which it falls is ruined.
entries.1cdd5deb17796a7cae2591314fb441c0cfab6624: <hi type="bold">Verse 39</hi> <div eID="gen30737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30738" type="x-p"/> The wild beasts of the desert - Dahler translates these various terms, "The wild cats, the jackals, and the ostriches." And Blayney the same. Wicklif, "Dragons, woodewoses, and ostriches." Coverdale, "Wild beestes, apes, and estriches."
entries.355bef8ab67484eb8dcdc485f689b4464ab310be: <hi type="bold">Verse 40</hi> <div eID="gen30738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30739" type="x-p"/> As God overthrew Sodom - As the very ground on which these cities stood, with all the plain, now lies under the Dead Sea; so Babylon and the adjacent country shall be rendered totally barren and unfruitful, and utterly incapable of being inhabited. And this is the fact concerning both countries. See <reference osisRef="Jer.49.18">Jer 49:18</reference>.
entries.ad720d7cd4449bd98c2f561cee477472affab562: <hi type="bold">Verse 41</hi> <div eID="gen30739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30740" type="x-p"/> Behold, a people shall come from the north - This and the two following verses are nearly the same with <reference osisRef="Jer.6.22-Jer.6.24">Jer 6:22-24</reference>. But here, destroyers against Babylon are intended; there, destroyers against Jerusalem.
entries.0fcddad6839cf35c46a6606bd4fbfa757944b478: <hi type="bold">Verse 44</hi> <div eID="gen30740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30741" type="x-p"/> Behold, he shall came up like a lion - The same words as in <reference osisRef="Jer.49.19">Jer 49:19</reference> (note), etc., where see the note.
entries.ffa9ede6401842053c20a7a0e3b0f2ad6d1e97e5: <hi type="bold">Verse 46</hi> <div eID="gen30741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30742" type="x-p"/> At the noise of the taking of Babylon - See the note on the parallel place, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.21">Jer 49:21</reference> (note). In the forty-ninth chapter, these words are spoken of Nebuchadnezzar; here, of Cyrus. The taking of Babylon was a wonder to all the surrounding nations. It was thought to be impregnable.  <chapter eID="Jer.50"/> <div eID="gen30742" type="x-p"/>

entries.1743d527bf8e07332e7005d60f177fee0380a543: <div eID="gen14440" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Against Babylon - Jeremiah 50-51</title> <div sID="gen14441" type="x-p"/> The genuineness of this prophecy has been impugned by the newer criticism in different ways; for some quite refuse to allow it as Jeremiah’s, while others consider it a mere interpolation.<note placement="foot">With regard to the special attacks and their refutation, see details on Keil’s <hi type="italic">Manual of Introduction to the Old Testament</hi> translated by Prof. Douglas, in Clark’s F.T.L. vol. i. p. 342ff.. To the list there given of the defenders of this prophecy (of whom Kueper, Hävernick, and Nägelsbach in the monograph entitled <hi type="italic">der Prophet Jeremias und Babylon</hi>, 1850, have thoroughly discussed the question), we must add the name of Graf, who, in the remarks prefixed to his commentary on Jer 50f., has thoroughly examined the arguments of his opponents, and reached this result: "The prophecy contains nothing which Jeremiah could not have written in the fourth year of Zedekiah; and the style of writing itself exhibits all the peculiarities which present themselves in his book. This prophecy is therefore as much his work as the prophecies against the other foreign nations." Only the passage <reference osisRef="Jer.51.15-Jer.51.19">Jer 51:15-19</reference>, a repetition of <reference osisRef="Jer.10.12-Jer.10.16">Jer 10:12-16</reference>, is said to proceed from another hand, because it stands out of all connection with what precedes and what follows it (but see the exposition); while he has so fully vindicated, as genuine portions of the prophecy, other passages which had been assumed as interpolations, even by Nägelsbach in his monograph, that the latter, in treating of Jeremiah in Lange’s <hi type="italic">Bibelwerk</hi> see Clark’s Translation, p. 419, has renounced his former doubts, and now declares that it is only the passage in <reference osisRef="Jer.51.15-Jer.51.19">Jer 51:15-19</reference> that he cannot regard as original.</note> <div eID="gen14441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14442" type="x-p"/> Hitzig (<hi type="italic">Exeg. Handb</hi>. 2 Aufl.) considers that this oracle, with its epilogue, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.59-Jer.51.64">Jer 51:59-64</reference>, is not to be wholly rejected as spurious, as has been done by Von Cölln and Gramberg; he is so much the less inclined to reject it, because, although there is many an interpolated piece here and there (?), yet no independent oracle has hitherto been found in Jeremiah that is wholly interpolated. "In fact," he continues, "this oracle shows numerous traces of its genuineness, and reasons for maintaining it. The use of particular words (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.6">Jer 50:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.1">Jer 51:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.5">Jer 51:5</reference>,<reference osisRef="Jer.51.7">Jer 51:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.14">Jer 51:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.45">Jer 51:45</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.55">Jer 51:55</reference>), and the circle of figures employed (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.7-Jer.51.8">Jer 51:7-8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.34">Jer 51:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.37">Jer 51:37</reference>), as well as the style (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.2-Jer.50.3">Jer 50:2-3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.7-Jer.50.8">Jer 50:7-8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.10">Jer 50:10</reference>), especially in turns like <reference osisRef="Jer.51.2">Jer 51:2</reference>; the concluding formula, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.57">Jer 51:57</reference>; the dialogue introduced without any forewarning, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.51">Jer 51:51</reference>, - all unmistakeably reveal Jeremiah; and this result is confirmed by chronological data." These chronological data, which Hitzig then extracts from particular verses, we cannot certainly esteem convincing, since they have been obtained through a method of exegesis which denies the spirit and the essential nature of prophecy; but his remarks concerning Jeremiah’s use of words and his circle of images are perfectly well-founded, and may be considerably corroborated if the matter were more minutely investigated. Notwithstanding all this, Ewald has again repeated, in the second edition of his work on the Prophets, the assertion first made by Eichhorn, that this prophecy is spurious. He does not, indeed, deny that "this long piece against Babylon has many words, turns of expression, and thoughts, nay, even the whole plan, in common with Jeremiah; and since Jeremiah is often accustomed in other places also to repeat himself, this might, at the first look, even create a prepossession favouring the opinion that it was composed by Jeremiah himself. But Jeremiah repeats himself in a more wholesale style, and is not unfaithful to himself in his repetitions: here, however, the Jeremianic element peers through only in single though very numerous passages, and the repeated portions are often completely transformed. What, therefore, appears here as Jeremianic is rather a studied repetition and imitation, which would require here to be all the stronger, when the piece was intended to pass as one of Jeremiah’s writings." Ewald goes on to say that Babylon appears already as directly threatened by Cyrus; and the whole view taken of Babylon as a kingdom utterly degenerated, and unable any longer to escape the final destruction, - the prophetic impetuosity shown in rising up against the Chaldean oppression, - the public summons addressed to all the brethren living in Babylon, that they should flee from the city, now irrecoverably lost, and return to the holy land, - the distinct mention of the Medes and other northern nations as the mortal enemies of Babylon, and of the speedy and certain fall of this city; - all this, says Ewald, is foreign to Jeremiah, nay, even conflicting and impossible. For particular proof of this sweeping verdict, Ewald refers to the name שׁשׁך (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.41">Jer 51:41</reference>, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.25.26">Jer 25:26</reference>) for Babylon, לב for כּשׂדּים, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.1">Jer 51:1</reference>, and similar circumlocutions for Chaldean names, Jer 51:21. He refers also to certain words which are quite new, and peculiar only to Ezekiel and later writers: סגן, פּחה, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.23">Jer 51:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.25">Jer 51:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.27">Jer 51:27</reference>; גּלּוּלים, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.2">Jer 50:2</reference>; בּדּים as a designation of false prophets, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.36">Jer 50:36</reference>; also to החרים, to devote with a curse, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.21">Jer 50:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.26">Jer 50:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.3">Jer 51:3</reference>, which in the rest of Jeremiah occurs only Jer 25:9. Further, he refers to the headings found in <reference osisRef="Jer.50.1">Jer 50:1</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.51.59">Jer 51:59</reference>, which are quite different from what Jeremiah himself would have written; and lastly, to the intimate connection subsisting between <reference osisRef="Jer.50.27">Jer 50:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.40">Jer 51:40</reference>, and Isa 34:6., between <reference osisRef="Jer.50.39">Jer 50:39</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.34.14">Isa 34:14</reference>, and between 51:60ff. and Jer 34:16. <div eID="gen14442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14443" type="x-p"/> But all these considerations are much too weak to prove the spuriousness of the passage before us. The connection with Isa 34 quite agrees with Jeremiah’s characteristic tendency to lean on older prophecies, and reproduce the thoughts contained in them (we merely recall the case of the prophecy concerning Moab in Jer 48, against whose genuineness even Ewald has nothing to say); and it can be brought to tell against the genuineness of this oracle only on the groundless supposition that Isa 34 originated in exile times. The headings given in <reference osisRef="Jer.50.1">Jer 50:1</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.51.59">Jer 51:59</reference> contain nothing whatever that would be strange in Jeremiah: <reference osisRef="Jer.51.59">Jer 51:59</reference> is not a title at all, but the commencement of the account regarding the charge which Jeremiah gave to Seraiah when he was going to Babylon, with reference to his carrying with him the prophecy concerning Babylon; and the heading in <reference osisRef="Jer.50.1">Jer 50:1</reference> almost exactly agrees with that in <reference osisRef="Jer.46.13">Jer 46:13</reference> (see the exposition). Of the alleged later words, החרים and גּלּוּלים are derived from the Pentateuch, בּדּים from Isa 44:25. סגן and פּחה certainly were not known to the Hebrews till the invasions of Judah by the Assyrians and Chaldeans; but he latter of the two words we find as early as in the address of the Assyrians in <reference osisRef="Isa.36.9">Isa 36:9</reference>, and the former in <reference osisRef="Isa.41.25">Isa 41:25</reference> : thus, not a single one of the words alleged to have been first used by Ezekiel is peculiar to him. Finally, of the circumlocutions used for the names "Babylon" and "Chaldeans," Ewald himself confesses that שׁשׁך in <reference osisRef="Jer.25.26">Jer 25:26</reference> may be Jeremiah's; and he has yet to give proof for the assertion that the names cited are merely circumlocutions in which a play is made on words that did not come into vogue till after Jeremiah’s time. And as little has been even attempted in the way of establishing the opinion he has expressed regarding what is Jeremianic in the prophecy, - that it is a studied repetition and imitation, - or the assertion that Babylon is represented as being directly threatened by Cyrus. In the Old Testament Scriptures, Cyrus is represented as the king of Persia, which he was; but this prophecy says nothing of the Persians. Thus, the learned supplementary matter with which Ewald seeks to support his general assertions is by no means fitted to strengthen his position, but rather shows that the proper argument for rejecting this oracle as spurious is not to be found in the nature of this particular prophecy, but in the axiom openly expressed by Eichhorn, von Cölln, Gramberg, and other followers of the "vulgar rationalism," that Jeremiah could not have announced the destruction of Babylon by the Medes, because at his time the Medes had not yet appeared on the scene of history as a conquering nation; for, according to the principles of rationalism, the prophets could merely prophesy of things which lay within the political horizon. It has not escaped the acute observation of Hitzig, that the genuineness of this prophecy could not be shaken by such general assertions; hence he has adopted Movers’ hypothesis of numerous interpolations, in order thereby to account for the use made of portions of Isaiah, which, on dogmatic grounds, are referred to the exile. But for this assumption also there are wanting proofs that can stand the test. Besides the general assertion that Jeremiah could not have repeated earlier prices word for word, the arguments which Movers and Hitzig bring forward from the context, or from a consideration of the contents, in the case of isolated verses, depend upon false renderings of words, conjectures of a merely subjective character, and misunderstandings of various kinds, which at once fall to the ground when the correct explanation is given. <div eID="gen14443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14444" type="x-p"/> The germ of this prophecy lies in the word of the Lord, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.12">Jer 25:12</reference>, "When seventy years are completed, I will punish the king of Babylon and that nation for their iniquity, and the land of the Chaldeans, and make it everlasting desolations;" and its position with regard to the other prophecies of Jeremiah against the nations has already been given in outline in the statement of <reference osisRef="Jer.25.26">Jer 25:26</reference>, "And the king of Sheshach (Babylon) shall drink after them." Just as these utterances (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.12">Jer 25:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.26">Jer 25:26</reference>) stand in full accord with the announcement that, in the immediate future, all nations shall be given into the power of the king of Babylon, and serve him seventy years; so, too, the prophecy against Babylon now lying before us not only does not stand in contradiction with the call addressed to Jeremiah, that he should proclaim to his contemporaries the judgment which Babylon is to execute on Judah and all nations, but it rather belongs to the complete solution of the problems connected with this call. The announcement of the fall of Babylon, and the release of Israel from Babylon, form the subject of the prophecy, which is more than a hundred verses in length. This double subject, the two parts of which are so closely connected, is portrayed in a series of images which, nearly throughout, are arranged pretty loosely together, so that it is impossible to summarize the rich and varied contents of these figures, and to sketch a correct plan of the course of thought and of the divisions of the oracle. Hence, too, the views of expositors with regard to the division of the whole into parts or strophes widely differ;<note placement="foot">Thus, according to Eichhorn, Dahler, and Rosenmüller, the whole consists of several pieces (three or six) which originally belonged to different periods; according to Schmieder, it consists of "seven different poems of songs, all having the same subject, which, however, they set forth from different sides, and under countless images." Nägelsbach at first assumed that there were three main divisions, with thirteen subdivisions; afterwards, in Lange’s <hi type="italic">Bibelwerk</hi> see Clark’s Foreign Theol. Library, he thinks he is able also to distinguish three stages of time, which, however, do not permit of being sharply defined, so that he continues to divide the whole prophecy into nineteen separate views or figures.</note> we follow the view of Ewald, that the whole falls into three main parts (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.2-Jer.50.28">Jer 50:2-28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.29">Jer 50:29</reference> on to <reference osisRef="Jer.51.26">Jer 51:26</reference>, and 51:27-58), every one of which begins with a spirited exhortation to engage in battle. These three main portions again fall into ten periods, of which the first three (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.2-Jer.50.10">Jer 50:2-10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.11-Jer.50.20">Jer 50:11-20</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Jer.50.21-Jer.50.28">Jer 50:21-28</reference>) form the first main division; the four middle ones form the second main portion (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.29-Jer.50.40">Jer 50:29-40</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.41">Jer 50:41</reference> to <reference osisRef="Jer.51.4">Jer 51:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.5-Jer.51.14">Jer 51:5-14</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Jer.51.15-Jer.51.26">Jer 51:15-26</reference>); while the following three form the last (vv. 27-37, 38-49, and 50-58). We further agree with what Ewald says regarding the contents of the first two parts in general, viz., that in the first the prevailing view is the necessity for the deliverance of Israel, and that in the second, the antithesis between Babylon on the one hand, and Jahveh together with Israel, His spiritual instrument, on the other, is fully brought out; but we do not agree with his remark concerning the third part, that there the prevailing feature is the detailed description of the condition of Israel at that time, for this does not at all agree with the contents of 51:27-58. Rather, the address rises into a triumphant description of the fall of Babylon, in which the Lord will show Himself as the avenger of His people. On the whole, then, the prophecy is neither wanting in arrangement nor in that necessary progress in the development of thought which proves unity of conception and execution. <div eID="gen14444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14445" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Jer.50.1">Jer 50:1</reference> The title, <hi type="italic">"The word which Jahveh spake concerning Babylon, concerning the land of the Chaldeans, by Jeremiah the prophet,"</hi> follows <reference osisRef="Jer.46.13">Jer 46:13</reference> in choosing אשׁר דּ instead of the usual אשׁר היה, and deviates from that passage only in substituting "by the hand of Jeremiah" for "to Jeremiah," as in Jer 37:2. The preference of the expression "spake by the hand of" for "spake to," is connected with the fact that the following prophecy does not contain a message of the Lord which came to Jeremiah, that he might utter it before the people, but a message which he was to write down and send to Babylon, Jer 51:60. The apposition to "Babylon," viz., "the land of the Chaldeans," serves the purpose of more exactly declaring that "Babylon" is to be understood not merely of the capital, but also of the kingdom; cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.50.8">Jer 50:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.45">Jer 50:45</reference>, and 51, 54.
entries.df80852f58b46bf718af4c874b120d4519f30f7a: <reference osisRef="Jer.50.2-Jer.50.10">Jer 50:2-10</reference> <hi type="italic">The fall of Babylon, and deliverance of Israel. - </hi> Jer 50:2. <hi type="italic">"Tell it among the nations, and cause it to be heard, and lift up a standard; cause it to be heard, conceal it not: say, Babylon is taken, Bel is ashamed, Merodach is confounded; her images are ashamed, her idols are confounded. </hi> Jer 50:3. <hi type="italic">For there hath come up against her a nation out of the north; it will make her land a desolation, and there shall be not an inhabitant in it: from man to beast, [all] have fled, are gone. </hi> Jer 50:4. <hi type="italic">In those days, and at that time, saith Jahveh, the children of Israel shall come, they and the children of Judah together; they shall go, weeping as they go, and shall seek Jahveh their God. </hi> Jer 50:5. <hi type="italic">They shall ask for Zion, with their faces [turned to] the road hitherwards, [saying], Come, and let us join ourselves to Jahveh by an eternal covenant [which] shall not be forgotten. </hi> Jer 50:6. <hi type="italic">My people have been a flock of lost ones; their shepherds have misled them [on] mountains which lead astray: from mountain to hill they went; they forgot their resting-place. </hi> Jer 50:7. <hi type="italic">All who found them have devoured them; and their enemies said, We are not guilty, for they have sinned against Jahveh, the dwelling-place of justice, and the hope of their fathers, Jahveh. </hi> Jer 50:8. <hi type="italic">Flee out of the midst of Babylon, and from the land of the Chaldeans; let them go forth, and let them be like he-goats before a flock. </hi> Jer 50:9. <hi type="italic">For, behold, I will stir up, and bring up against Babylon, an assembly of great nations out of the land of the north: and they shall array themselves against her; on that side shall she be taken: his arrows [are] like [those of] a skilful hero [who] does not return empty. </hi> Jer 50:10. <hi type="italic">And [the land of the] Chaldeans shall become a spoil; all those who spoil her shall be satisfied, saith Jahveh."</hi> <div eID="gen14445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14446" type="x-p"/> In the spirit Jeremiah sees the fall of Babylon, together with its idols, as if it had actually taken place, and gives the command to proclaim among the nations this event, which brings deliverance for Israel and Judah. The joy over this is expressed in the accumulation of the words for the summons to tell the nations what has happened. On the expression, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.4.5-Jer.4.6">Jer 4:5-6</reference>; Jer 46:14. The lifting up of a standard, i.e., of a signal-rod, served for the more rapid spreading of news; cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.4.6">Jer 4:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.6.1">Jer 6:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.13.2">Isa 13:2</reference>, etc. "Cause it to be heard" is intensified by the addition of "do not conceal it." The thing is to be proclaimed without reserve; cf. Jer 38:14. "Babylon is taken," i.e., conquered, and her idols have become ashamed, inasmuch as, from their inability to save their city, their powerlessness and nullity have come to light. Bel and Merodach are not different divinities, but merely different names for the chief deity of the Babylonians. Bel = Baal, the Jupiter of the Babylonians, was, as Bel-merodach, the tutelary god of Babylon. "The whole of the Babylonian dynasty," says Oppert, <hi type="italic">Expéd. en Mésopot</hi>. ii. p. 272, "places him [Merodach] at the head of the gods; and the inscription of Borsippa calls him the king of heaven and earth." עצבּים, "images of idols," and גּלּוּלים, properly "logs," an expression of contempt for idols (see on <reference osisRef="Lev.26.30">Lev 26:30</reference>), are synonymous ideas for designating the nature and character of the Babylonian gods.
entries.1681b23beeab36e5c22eb6637c6c84a138e4156f: <reference osisRef="Jer.50.11-Jer.50.20">Jer 50:11-20</reference> <hi type="italic">The devastation of Babylon and glory of Israel.  -</hi> Jer 50:11. <hi type="italic">"Thou ye rejoice, though ye exult, O ye plunderers of mine inheritance, though ye leap proudly like a heifer threshing, and neigh like strong horses,</hi> Jer 50:12. <hi type="italic">Your mother will be very much ashamed; she who bare you will blush: behold, the last of the nations [will be] a wilderness, a desert, and a steppe.</hi> Jer 50:13. <hi type="italic">Because of the indignation of Jahveh it shall not be inhabited, and it shall become a complete desolation. Every one passing by Babylon will be astonished, and hiss because of all her plagues.</hi> Jer 50:14. <hi type="italic">Make preparations against Babylon round about, all ye that bend the bow; shoot at her, do not spare an arrow, for she hath sinned against Jahveh.</hi> Jer 50:15. <hi type="italic">Shout against her round about; she hath given herself up: her battlements are fallen, her walls are pulled down; for it is Jahveh’s vengeance: revenge yourselves on her; as she hath done, do ye to her.</hi> Jer 50:16. <hi type="italic">Cut off the sower from Babylon, and him that handles the sickle in the time of harvest. From before the oppressing sword each one will turn to his own nation, and each one will flee to his own land.</hi> Jer 50:17. <hi type="italic">Israel is a scattered sheep [which] lions have driven away: the first [who] devoured him [was] the king of Babylon; and this, the last, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, hath broken his bones.</hi> Jer 50:18. <hi type="italic">Therefore thus saith Jahveh of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will punish the king of Babylon ad his land, as I have punished the king of Assyria.</hi> Jer 50:19. <hi type="italic">And I will bring back Israel to his pasture-ground, and he shall feed on Carmel and Bashan, and on the mountains of Ephraim his soul shall be satisfied.</hi> Jer 50:20. <hi type="italic">In those days, and at that time, saith Jahveh, the iniquity of Israel shall be sought for, but it shall not be; and the sins of Judah, but they shall not be found: for I will pardon those whom I will leave remaining."</hi>  <reference osisRef="Jer.50.11-Jer.50.13">Jer 50:11-13</reference> <div eID="gen14453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14454" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Jer.50.11">Jer 50:11</reference> does not permit of being so closely connected with what precedes as to separate it from <reference osisRef="Jer.50.12">Jer 50:12</reference> (De Wette, Nägelsbach). Not only is the translation, "for thou didst rejoice," etc., difficult to connect with the imperfects of all the verbs in the verse, but the direct address also does not suit <reference osisRef="Jer.50.10">Jer 50:10</reference>, and rather demands connection with <reference osisRef="Jer.50.12">Jer 50:12</reference>, where it is continued. כּי, of course, introduces the reason, yet not in such a way that <reference osisRef="Jer.50.11">Jer 50:11</reference> states the cause why Chaldea shall become a spoil, but rather so that <reference osisRef="Jer.50.11">Jer 50:11</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.50.12">Jer 50:12</reference> together give the reason for the threatening uttered. The different clauses of <reference osisRef="Jer.50.11">Jer 50:11</reference> are the protases, to which <reference osisRef="Jer.50.12">Jer 50:12</reference> brings the apodosis. "You may go on making merry over the defeat of Israel, but shame will follow for this." The change of the singular forms of the verbs into plurals (<hi type="italic">Qeri</hi>) has been caused by the plural 'שׁסי , but is unnecessary, because Babylon is regarded as a collective, and its people are gathered into the unity of a person; see on Jer 13:20. "Spoilers of mine inheritance," i.e., of the people and land of the Lord; cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.12.7">Jer 12:7</reference>; Isa 17:14. On פּוּשׁ, to gallop (of a horse, <reference osisRef="Hab.1.8">Hab 1:8</reference>), hop, spring (of a calf, Mal. 3:20), see on Hab 1:8. דּשׁא is rendered by the lxx ἐν βοτάνη, by the Vulgate <hi type="italic">super herbam</hi>; after these, Ewald also takes the meaning of springing like a calf through the grass, since he explains דּשׁא  as exhibiting the correct punctuation, and remarks that פּוּשׁ, like הלך, can stand with an object directly after it; see §282, <hi type="italic">a</hi>. Most modern expositors, on the other hand, take דּשׁא as the fem. participle from דּוּשׁ, written with א instead of ה: "like a threshing heifer." On this, A Schultens, in his <hi type="italic">Animadv. philol.</hi>, on this passage, remarks: <hi type="italic">Comparatio petita est a vitula, quae in area media inter frumenta, ore ex lege non ligato</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.25.10">Deu 25:10</reference>), <hi type="italic">prae pabuli abundantia gestit ex exsultat</hi>. This explanation also gives a suitable meaning, without compelling us to do violence to the language and to alter the text. As to אבּירים, stallions, strong horses (Luther), see on <reference osisRef="Jer.8.16">Jer 8:16</reference> and Jer 47:3. "Your mother" is the whole body of the people, the nation considered as a unity (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.50.1">Isa 50:1</reference>; Hos 2:4; Hos 4:5), the individual members of which are called her sons; cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.5.7">Jer 5:7</reference>, etc. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Jer.50.12">Jer 50:12</reference></hi>, the disgrace that is to fall on Babylon is more distinctly specified. The thought is gathered up into a sententious saying, in imitation of the sayings of Balaam. "The last of the nations" is the antithesis of "the first of the nations," as Balaam calls Amalek, Num 24:20, because they were the first heathen nation that began to fight against the people of Israel. In like manner, Jeremiah calls Babylon the last of the heathen nations. As the end of Amalek is ruin (Num 24:20), so the end of the last heathen nation that comes forward against Israel will be a wilderness, desert, steppe. The predicates (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.2.6">Jer 2:6</reference>) refer to the country and kingdom of Babylon. But if the end of the kingdom is a desert, then the people must have perished. The devastation of Babylon is further portrayed in <reference osisRef="Jer.50.13">Jer 50:13</reference>, together with a statement of the cause: "Because of the anger of Jahveh it shall not be inhabited;" cf. Isa 13:20. The words from והיתה onwards are imitated from <reference osisRef="Jer.49.17">Jer 49:17</reference> and Jer 19:8.
entries.6e8709ce9bcdd5cfc83669e13373737d08aecf3a: <reference osisRef="Jer.50.21-Jer.50.28">Jer 50:21-28</reference> <div eID="gen14457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14458" type="x-p"/> The pride and power of Babylon are broken, as a punishment for the sacrilege he committed at the temple of the Lord. Jer 50:21. <hi type="italic">"Against the land, - Double-rebellion, - go up against it, and against the inhabitants of visitation; lay waste and devote to destruction after them, saith Jahveh, and do according to all that I have commanded thee. </hi> Jer 50:22. <hi type="italic">A sound of war [is] in the land, and great destruction. </hi> Jer 50:23. <hi type="italic">How the hammer of the whole earth is cut and broken! how Babylon has become a desolation among the nations! </hi> Jer 50:24. <hi type="italic">I laid snares for thee, yea, and thou hast been taken, O Babylon; but thou didst not know: thou wast found, and also seized, because thou didst strive against Jahveh. </hi> Jer 50:25. <hi type="italic">Jahveh hath opened His treasure-house, and brought out the instruments of His wrath; for the Lord, Jahveh of hosts, hath a work in the land of the Chaldeans. </hi> Jer 50:26. <hi type="italic">Come against her, [all of you], from the last to the first; open her storehouses: case her up in heaps, like ruins, and devote her to destruction; let there be no remnant left to her. </hi> Jer 50:27. <hi type="italic">Destroy all her oxen; let them go down to the slaughter: woe to them! for their day is come, the time of their visitation. </hi> Jer 50:28. <hi type="italic">[There is] a sound of those who flee and escape out of the land of Babylon, to declare in Zion the vengeance of Jahveh our God, the vengeance of His temple."</hi> <div eID="gen14458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14459" type="x-p"/> The punishment of Babylon will be fearful, corresponding to its crimes. The crimes of Babylon and its punishment Jeremiah has comprised, in <reference osisRef="Jer.50.21">Jer 50:21</reference>, in two names specially formed for the occasion. The enemy to whom God has entrusted the execution of the punishment is to march against the land מרתים. This word, which is formed by the prophet in a manner analogous to <hi type="italic">Mizraim</hi>, and perhaps also <hi type="italic">Aram Naharaim</hi>, means "double rebellion," or "double obstinacy." It comes from the root מרה, "to be rebellious" against Jahveh and His commandments, whence also מרי, "rebellion;" Num 17:1-13 :25, <reference osisRef="Ezek.2.5">Eze 2:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.2.7">Eze 2:7</reference>, etc. Other interpretations of the word are untenable: such is that of Fürst, who follows the Vulgate "<hi type="italic">terram dominantium</hi>," and, comparing the Aramaic מרא, "Lord," renders it by "dominion" (<hi type="italic">Herschaft</hi>). Utterly indefensible, too, is the translation of Hitzig, "the world of men" (<hi type="italic">Menschenwelt</hi>), which he derives from the Sanskrit <hi type="italic">martjam</hi>, "world," on the basis of the false assumption that the language of the Chaldeans was Indo-Germanic. The only doubtful points are in what respect Babylon showed double obstinacy, and what Jeremiah had in his mind at the time. The view of Hitzig, Maurer, Graf, etc., is certainly incorrect, - that the prophet was thinking of the double punishment of Israel by the Assyrians and by the Babylonians (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.17">Jer 50:17</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.50.33">Jer 50:33</reference>); for the name is evidently given to the country which is now about to be punished, and hence to the power of Babylon. Nägelsbach takes a twofold view: (1) he thinks of the defiance shown by Babylon towards both man and God; (2) he thinks of the double obstinacy it exhibited in early times by building the tower, and founding the first worldly kingdom (Gen 10:8.), and in later times by its conduct towards the theocracy: and he is inclined rather to the latter than to the former view, because the offences committed by Babylon in early and in later times were, in their points of origin and aim, too much one and the same for any one to be able to represent them as falling under two divisions. This is certainly correct; but against the first view there is also the important consideration that מרה is pretty constantly used only of opposition to God and the word of God. If any one, notwithstanding this, is inclined to refer the name also to offences against men, he could yet hardly agree with Nägelsbach in thinking of the insurrections of Babylon against the kings of Assyria, their masters; for these revolts had no meaning in reference to the position of Babylon towards God, but rather showed the haughty spirit in which Babylon trod on all the nations. <div eID="gen14459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14460" type="x-p"/> The opinion of Dahler has most in its favour: "Doubly rebellious, i.e., more rebellious than others, through its idolatry ad its pride, which was exalted it against God, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.24">Jer 50:24</reference>, Jer 50:29." Rosenmüller, De Wette, etc., have decided in favour of this view. Although the dual originally expresses the idea of pairing, yet the Hebrew associates with <hi type="italic">double, twofold</hi>, the idea of increase, gradation; cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.40.2">Isa 40:2</reference>; Isa 66:7. The object is prefixed for the sake of emphasis; and in order to render it still more prominent, it is resumed after the verb in the expression "against it." פּקוד, an infinitive in form, "to visit with punishment, avenge, punish," is also used as a significant name of Babylon: the land that visits with punishment is to be punished. Many expositors take חרב as a denominative from חרב, "sword," in the sense of strangling, murdering; so also in Jer 50:27. But this assumption is far from correct; nor is there any need for making it, because the meaning of destroying is easily obtained from that of being laid waste, or destroying oneself by transferring the word from things to men. החרים, "to proscribe, put under the ban," and in effect "to exterminate;" see on Jer 25:9. On "after them," cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.49.37">Jer 49:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.48.2">Jer 48:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.9">Jer 48:9</reference>,<reference osisRef="Jer.48.15">Jer 48:15</reference>, etc.
entries.347244066f348a555512d3826e3a1ff51e0cb959: <reference osisRef="Jer.50.29-Jer.50.40">Jer 50:29-40</reference> <div eID="gen14463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14464" type="x-p"/> The pride of Babylon is humbled through the utter destruction of the people and the land. - Jer 50:29. <hi type="italic">"Summon archers against Jerusalem, all those who bend the bow; encamp against her round about. Let there be no escape for her; recompense to her according to her work; according to that which she hath done, do ye to her: for she hath presumed against Jahveh, against the Holy One of Israel. </hi> Jer 50:30. <hi type="italic">Therefore shall her young men fall in her streets, and all her men of war shall fail in that day, saith Jahveh. </hi> Jer 50:31. <hi type="italic">Behold, I am against thee, O Pride! said the Lord, Jahveh of hosts; for thy day hath come, the time [when] I visit thee. </hi> Jer 50:32. <hi type="italic">And Pride shall stumble and fall, and he shall have none to lift him up; and I will kindle fire in his cities, and it shall devour all that is round about him. </hi> Jer 50:33. <hi type="italic">Thus saith Jahveh of hosts, the Children of Israel and the children of Judah are oppressed together, and all who led them captive kept hold of them; they refused to let them go. </hi> Jer 50:34. <hi type="italic">Their Redeemer is strong; Jahveh of hosts is His name: He shall surely plead their cause, that He may give rest to the earth, and make the inhabitants of Babylon tremble. </hi> Jer 50:35. <hi type="italic">A sword [is] against the Chaldeans, saith Jahveh, and against the inhabitants of Babylon, and against her princes, and against her wise men. </hi> Jer 50:36. <hi type="italic">A sword [is] against the liars, and they shall become fools; a sword is against her heroes, and they shall be confounded. </hi> Jer 50:37. <hi type="italic">A sword [is] against his horses, and against his chariots, and against all the auxiliaries which [are] in the midst of her, and they shall become women; a sword is against her treasures, and they shall be plundered. </hi> Jer 50:38. <hi type="italic">A drought is against her waters, and they shall become dry; for it is a land of graven images, and they are mad upon idols. </hi> Jer 50:39. <hi type="italic">Therefore shall wild beasts dwell [there] with jackals, and ostriches shall dwell in it; and it shall no more be inhabited for ever, neither shall it be dwelt in from generation to generation. </hi> Jer 50:40. <hi type="italic">As God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah and their inhabitants, saith Jahveh, no man shall dwell there, nor shall a son of man sojourn in it."</hi> <div eID="gen14464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14465" type="x-p"/> Further description of the execution of God’s wrath. Archers shall come and besiege Babylon round about, so that no one shall escape. The summons, "Call archers hither," is a dramatic turn in the thought that the siege is quickly to ensue. השׁמיע is used here as in <reference osisRef="Jer.51.27">Jer 51:27</reference>, to summon, call by making proclamation, as in 1Ki 15:22. רבּים does not signify "many," as the ancient versions give it; this agrees neither with the apposition which follows, "all that bend the bow," nor with <reference osisRef="Jer.50.26">Jer 50:26</reference>, where all, to the last, are summoned against Babylon. Raschi, followed by all the moderns, more correctly renders it "archers," and derives it from רבה = רבב, <reference osisRef="Gen.49.23">Gen 49:23</reference>, cf. with <reference osisRef="Jer.21.10">Jer 21:10</reference>, like רב, Job 16:13. The apposition, "all those who bend the bow," gives additional force. חנה with accus. means to besiege; cf. Psa 53:6. "Let there be no escape" is equivalent to saying, "that none may escape from Babylon." The <hi type="italic">Qeri</hi> להּ after יהי is unnecessary, and merely taken from Jer 50:26. On the expression "render to her," etc., cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.25.14">Jer 25:14</reference>; and on "according to all," etc., f. Jer 50:15. "For she hath acted presumptuously against Jahveh," by burning His temple, and keeping His people captive: in this way has Babylon offended "against the Holy One of Israel." This epithet of God is taken from Isaiah, cf. Isa 51:5. This presumption must be punished.
entries.5074be3ceef99712b125ecd4269b8e307702dfd7: <reference osisRef="Jer.50.41-Jer.50.46">Jer 50:41-46</reference> <hi type="italic">The agents who execute the judgment. - </hi> Jer 50:41. <hi type="italic">"Behold, a people shall come from the north, and a great nation, and many kings shall be raised up from the most distant sides of the earth. </hi> Jer 50:42. <hi type="italic">Bow and javelin shall they seize: they are cruel, and will not pity; their voice shall sound like the sea, and they shall ride upon horses, [each one] arrayed like a man for the battle, against thee, O daughter of Babylon. </hi> Jer 50:43. <hi type="italic">The king of Babylon hath heard the report concerning them, and his hands have fallen down: distress hath seized him, writing pain, like [that of] the woman in childbirth. </hi> Jer 50:44. <hi type="italic">Behold, he shall come up like a lion from the glory of Jordan to a habitation of rock; but in a moment will I make them run away from her, and will set over her him who is chosen: for who is like me, and who will appoint me a time [to plead my defence]? and what shepherd [is there] that will stand before me? </hi> Jer 50:45. <hi type="italic">Therefore hear ye the counsel of Jahveh which He hath taken against Babylon, and His purposes which He hath purposed against the land of the Chaldeans: Assuredly they shall drag them away, the smallest of the flock; assuredly [their] habitation shall be astonished at them. </hi> Jer 50:46. <hi type="italic">At the cry, 'Babylon is taken,' the earth is shaken, and a cry [for help] is heard among the nations. "Thus saith Jahveh: Behold, I will stir up against Babylon, and against the inhabitants of [as it were] the heart of mine opponents, the spirit of a destroyer. </hi> Jer 51:2. <hi type="italic">And I will send against Babylon strangers, and they shall winnow her, and empty her land, because they are against her round about in a day of evil. </hi> Jer 51:3. <hi type="italic">Against [him who] bends let the bender bend his bow, and against [him who] lifts up himself in his coat of mail: and do not spare her young men; devote to destruction all her host, </hi> Jer 51:4. <hi type="italic">That slain ones may fall in the land of the Chaldeans, and those that are pierced through in her streets."</hi> <div eID="gen14469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14470" type="x-p"/> The greater portion of this strophe consists of quotations from former utterances. <reference osisRef="Jer.51.41-Jer.51.43">Jer 51:41-43</reference> are taken from <reference osisRef="Jer.6.22-Jer.6.24">Jer 6:22-24</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Jer.51.44-Jer.51.46">Jer 51:44-46</reference> from <reference osisRef="Jer.49.19-Jer.49.21">Jer 49:19-21</reference>; here they are applied to Babylon. What is said in <reference osisRef="Jer.6.22-Jer.6.24">Jer 6:22-24</reference> concerning the enemy out of the north who will devastate Judah, is here transferred to the enemy that is to destroy Babylon. For this purpose, after the words "and a great nation," are added "and many kings," in order to set forth the hostile army advancing against Babylon as one composed of many nations; and in consequence of this extension of the subject, the verb יערוּ is used in the plural, and אכזרי is changed into אכזרי המּה. Moreover, the mention of the "daughter of Babylon" instead of the "daughter of Zion" is attended by a change from the directly communicative form of address in the first person ("We have heard," etc., <reference osisRef="Jer.51.43">Jer 51:43</reference>) into the third person ("The king of Babylon hath heard," etc.). In applying the expression used in <reference osisRef="Jer.49.19-Jer.49.21">Jer 49:19-21</reference> regarding the instrument chosen for the destruction of Edom, to the instrument selected against Babylon (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.44-Jer.51.46">Jer 51:44-46</reference>), the names "Babylon" and "and land of the Chaldeans" are substituted for "Edom" and "the inhabitants of Teman" (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.20">Jer 49:20</reference>); but beyond this, only the last verse is changed, in accordance with the change of circumstances. The thought that, in consequence of the fall of Edom, the earth trembles, and Edom’s cry of anguish is heard on the Red Sea, is intensified thus: by the sound or cry, "Babylon is taken," the earth is shaken, and a cry is heard among the nations. The conquest of Babylon, the mistress of the world, puts the whole world in anxiety and fear, while the effects of Edom’s fall extend only to the Red Sea. The <hi type="italic">Kethib</hi> ארוצם, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.44">Jer 51:44</reference>, seems to come from the verb רצץ, in the sense of pushing, so that it is not a mere error in transcription for אריצם. Moreover, such changes made on former utterances, when they are repeated and applied to Babylon, show that these verses are not glosses which a reader has written on the margin, and a later copyist inserted into the text, but that Jeremiah himself has applied these earlier words in his address against Babylon. The two passages are not merely quite appropriately arranged beside one another, but even present in their connection a thought which has not hitherto been met with in the address against Babylon, and which does not recur afterwards. The enemy that is to conquer Babylon is certainly pointed out, so early as v. 9, as an assemblage of great nations out of the north, but not more particularly characterized there; but the nations that are to constitute the hostile army are not further designated till <reference osisRef="Jer.51.11">Jer 51:11</reference> and Jer 51:27. The second quotation, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.44-Jer.51.46">Jer 51:44-46</reference>, adds the new thought that the appearance of this enemy against Babylon is owing to a decree of the Lord, the execution of which no man can prevent, because there is none like Jahveh. The figurative description of the enemy as a lion coming up out of the thicket of reeds at the Jordan, frightening the herd feeding on their pasture-ground, and carrying off the weakly sheep, is appropriate both to Nebuchadnezzar’s expedition against Edom, and to the invasion of Babylonia by the Medes and their allies, for the purpose of laying waste the country of the Chaldeans, smiting the inhabitants of Babylon, and conquering it. Even the expression נוה permits of being applied to Babylonia, which was protected by its canal system and the strong walls of its capital.  <chapter eID="Jer.50"/> <div eID="gen14470" type="x-p"/>

entries.b9a47e22324ba531424ef9cd55b938a039f90b85:
Our Prophet has been hitherto speaking of neighboring nations who had cruelly harassed the chosen people; and it was some consolation when the children of Abraham understood that God undertook their cause and would be the avenger of those wrongs which they had suffered. But this of itself would have been no great consolation, yea, it might have been viewed as nothing by many, while there was no hope of restoration; for it would have been but a small consolation to have others as associates in misery. If, indeed, Jeremiah had only taught that none of the nations who had troubled God’s Church would escape unpunished, the Jews might have raised an objection, and said, that they were not freed from their own calamities, because the monarchy of Babylon still flourished, and that they were buried as it were in a perpetual grave. It was therefore necessary that what we read here should be predicted. And though this prophecy is given last, we ought to notice that the Prophet had from the beginning expressly spoken, as we have seen, of the calamity and destruction of Babylon. But this prophecy is given as the conclusion of the book, to mitigate the sorrow of the miserable exiles; for it was no small relief to them to hear that the tyranny by which they were oppressed, and under which they did live as it were a lifeless life, would not be perpetual. We now then understand why the Prophet spoke of the Babylonians and of their destruction.
