We now perceive the meaning of the words, — that the Babylonians would have to do, not with an idle but a terrible enemy, and with one who would surmount all obstacles, as when fury excites a lion when necessity drives him as it were headlong.
What follows is obscure. Some render the words thus, “When I shall make Israel to rest, then I will make them to flee from her.” In the former place (Jeremiah 49:19), we read “him,” in the singular, אריצנו, aritsnu; but here the Prophet uses the plural number, “them,” אריצם, aritsem; it is yet certain that the meaning is the same. Some, at the same time, apply this to the Jews, that God would remove them from Babylon, purposing to give them rest, that is, by dwelling securely in their own country; but as there is no mention made here of his people, this view is forced and far-fetched. I omit other explanations, for the meaning of the Prophet seems to me to be simply this, When I shall make an irruption, or, after I shall have made them rest, I will make them to flee He speaks, as I think, of the Chaldeans; and the particle כי, ki, is to be taken as an adverb of time, when, or after. It is, indeed, often a causative, but it has sometimes this meaning.
Now, these two clauses may be thus explained: When I shall make an irruption, or, when I shall have made them rest; for רגע, rego, means both to break and to rest. It is here in the active or causative conjugation, in Hiphil. If, then, we read, “After I shall have made them to rest,” the sense will be that the: Babylonians had been long tranquil, as there was no one who infested them or disturbed their peace; and we know that men having long rested in their idleness and sloth, become almost stupefied, so that they are touched with no fear. God then shows that the Babylonians were greatly mistaken, if they thought that the rest which they had previously enjoyed would be perpetual; for he would make them to flee from the city, though they had been long there in a tranquil state. The other sense is by no means unsuitable, “When I shall break,” or make an irruption, then all will flee away, that is, leave the city, which was before like a paradise. There is still no doubt but that the Prophet here denounces on the Babylonians a sudden overthrow, which would drive the people here and there in all directions.
See note on Jeremiah 49:19. — Ed.
It now follows, Who is the chosen one whom I shall set over her? God here in a manner deliberates as to the person whom he should make the leader of the war against the Chaldeans; and by these words he intimates that there would be ready for him the best general, and one especially active and also excelling in the art of war. And we know that even the unwilling are made to serve God, when he employs the ungodly as his scourges. In short, God shows that though the Babylonians might have brave leaders and most skillful in war, there yet would be prepared leaders, to whom he would commit the office of taking that city. And thus he teaches us at the same time that men are ruled by his hand, so that he chooses them according to his will and directs them to any work he pleases, Who is the chosen one, he says, whom I shall set over her?
And he adds, and who is like me? Here the Prophet shows that the Babylonians in vain trusted in their own defenses; for after having tried all things, they would find that whatever was set up against God and his invincible power, would be mere smoke. This sentence often occurs; and however common it may appear, yet, if we examine ourselves, we shall find that the Holy Spirit does not so often enforce it without reason; for after we have confessed that none is equal to God or can add to his power, — as soon as any trial assails us, this confession vanishes, and we tremble as though God was nothing, and had no power to bring us help. Diffidence, then, which often creeps in when we are in difficulties or dangers, sufficiently shows that we do not attribute to God the praise due to his power. He does not then exclaim here, as in other places, without reason, Who is like me? as though he had said, that the Babylonians would foolishly seek auxiliaries here and there; for when they had made the utmost exertions, whatever they might think the most useful would all vanish away, so that they would be destitute of all remedies.
He adds, And who will protest against me? Some give this frigid version, Who will prescribe to me the time? but they wholly pervert the meaning of the Prophet; for God in this place declares, that men would in vain contend or litigate with him. It is the same as if he had said, “Though all men were to rise up against, me, yet I will not allow them to litigate with me; and this they would also do in vain.” In short, God intimates that men would in vain clamor against his judgments, for he would nevertheless perform what he has decreed. He does not yet claim for himself that absolute power about which the sophists prattle, while they separate it from justice; but he intimates that the causes are not always manifest to men when he executes his judgments; for it is not without reason that the Scripture testifies that God’s judgments are a deep abyss; but by such an expression it is not meant that anything in God’s judgments is confused or in disorder, what then? even that God works in an extraordinary manner, and that hence his judgments are sometimes hidden from men.
Then God briefly shows, that though the Babylonians were to dispute, and start many objections, all this would be useless, because he would execute what he had decreed, and that without debating.
Let us then learn from these words, that when God’s works have the appearance of being unreasonable, we ought humbly to admire them, and never to judge them according to our computation; for God is not to be judged by us. Therefore, as I have already said, we are then only wise, when we humbly adore him in all his works, without disputing with him; for when we adduce all possible things, he will close our mouth with one word, and check all our presumption; nay, he will ever overcome us by being silent, for his justice will always overthrow whatever may come to our minds. But we must bear in mind what I have stated, that God never so acts by his absolute power as to separate it from his justice; for this would be as it were to wound himself; for these things are undivided, his power and justice, though justice often does not appeal however this may be, his sole and simple will is to us the rule of all justice.
It follows, And who is that shepherd who will stand before me? He alludes to the similitude he had used, for he compared himself before to a lion. he says now, “Since I shall go against Babylon like a lion, what shepherd will dare to oppose me?” We see that there is to be understood a contrast, between a lion and a shepherd; for God would be like a lion to destroy Babylon; hence, by pastor, he denotes any adversary who might come forth to defend the Chaldean flock. It follows, —
Jeremiah 50:45
45. Therefore hear ye the counsel of the LORD, that he hath taken against Babylon; and his purposes, that he hath purposed against the land of the Chaldeans: Surely the least of the flock shall draw them out: surely he shall make their habitation desolate with them.
45. Propterea audite consilium Jehovae quod consultavit contra Babylonem, et cogitationes quas cogitavit contra terram Chaldaeorum; Si non traxerint eos parvuli gregis; si non perdiderint super eos habitaculum.
entries.621f7c2a5c89d78c2d0883ad1524bf4aa590b128:
The Prophet confirms his previous doctrine, and uses an oath, for he had already spoken sufficiently at large of the destruction of Babylon, and his words might seem otherwise superfluous, because the subject had been explained with abundant clearness. But he introduces God here as making an oath, for the particles, “if not,” אם לא, am la, show the sentence to be elliptical; and we know that this form of swearing is common in Scripture. Then God swears, that the Babylonians were already given up to destruction, so that even the least of the flock would be superior to them.
But it is not without reason that the Prophet speaks here of the counsel of God and of his thoughts; for we know that men through their own vanity are held suspended or in doubt, so that they do not firmly acquiesce in God’s word, at least they vacillate so as to have no stability of faith. As, then, men think in themselves that possibly a thing may happen otherwise than according to the words of the prophets, Jeremiah does here meet such thoughts, and bids men to hear the counsel of God and his thoughts. It is, indeed, a mode of speaking transferred from men, when he speaks of the thoughts of God; for we know that God does not deliberate on what he is about to do, as the case is with men. But this manner of speaking so frequently occurs, that it ought to be familiar to us. However this may be, he intimates that God did not in vain announce terror when speaking of Babylon, but that the irrevocable decree was declared which God had formed. Hence he says, that he had already taken counsel, so that men need not deliberate any more, nor call into question his fixed decree, nor dispute concerning his thoughts. There is, then, no reason for men to revolve things in themselves, and to adopt different views; because events must be, he says, as I have predicted; God then has commanded me to announce this prophecy as brought forth from his counsel, which can by no means be changed. This is the reason why he mentions God’s counsel and thoughts.
He adds, If they shall not draw them forth; some read, “cast them out.” But סחב, sacheb, means to draw; and there is no doubt but that the Prophet denotes by this verb contempt and reproach; as carcasses are drawn through the mud, or a dead dog is drawn and cast into a river; so now, he says, Draw forth the Babylonians shall the least of the flock But how can these things agree together, that there was to be the choicest leader, and that yet the least of the flock would be the conquerors? God intimates, that though he would endow Cyrus with warlike valor, yet if it pleased him, there would be means by which he could destroy the Babylonians, were he to send sheep or lambs as their enemies. He means, in a word, that the Babylonians would be unwarlike, when God deprived them of their courage.
If they will not upset over them their tabernacle Some read as though the verb were שום, shum, “If they will not set,” etc.; others derive the word from ישם, ishem; but it comes rather from שמם, shemem; If, then, they will not upset over them their tabernacle, that is, when the Babylonians shall be laid prostrate, even their houses shall fall and overwhelm them. In short, God sets forth here a final ruin, from which the Babylonians could never be restored; for it is an evidence of hopeless despair, when houses are upset, so that their masters are buried in their ruins. It follows, —
Jeremiah 50:46
46. At the noise of the taking of Babylon the earth is moved, and the cry is heard among the nations.
46. A voce captae Babylonis contremuit terra, et clamor in gentibus, (vel, per gentes,) auditus est.
entries.58eac2f856dda1c13df4b406a02752e5786687be:
This is to anticipate an objection; for many might have said, “How can it be, that Babylon should thus fall, on whose monarchy so many and so wide countries are dependent?” As, then, such an event appearing so unreasonable, might occur to them, the Prophet meets the objection, and answers by way of anticipation, that though the earth shook, yet this would surely take place. He shows, at the same time, how great the calamity would be, for it would, by its noise, make the whole world to tremble: it would be thus better known how grievous was to be God’s vengeance on the Babylonians; for it was not to be without the shaking of the whole earth. Now follows, —
CHAPTER 51
Jeremiah 51:1
1. Thus saith the LORD; Behold, I will raise up against Babylon, and against them that dwell in the midst of them that rise up against me, a destroying wind;
1. Sic dicit Jehova, Ecce, ego excitans contra Babylonem, et contra habitatores cordis qui insurgunt contra me, venturn corrumpentem (vel, dissipantem.)

               <ns0:p n="7">7 All that found them have devoured them <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">As they be in the condition of lost sheep, so they have been under the fate of lost sheep, which every Dog, Fox<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Wolf de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vours.</ns0:note>, and their adversaries said, We offend not, because they have sinned against the LORD <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">And those that are their Enemies have pretended that in destroying them they have done no ill because they had sinned, so as the sins of the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> did both expose them to the Wrath of God, and also emboldned their Enemies, and encouraged them to think that they did God Service in destroying them.</ns0:note>, the habi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tation of justice <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>The habitation of Iustice.</ns0:hi> Some think this is a name here given to God, who indeed is the habitation of Justice, but whether the <ns0:hi>Chaldeans</ns0:hi> would call him so may be a question. Others therefore think the preposition <ns0:hi>in</ns0:hi> is understood, making this the aggravation of the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> sins, that they were committed in a land which ought to have been an habitation of Justice, as <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 26.10. it is said that the wicked man <ns0:hi>in a land of uprightness will deal unjustly.</ns0:hi> Mr. <ns0:hi>Calvin</ns0:hi> hath another notion, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> That the Prophet here incourageth him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self against what the Adversaries had promised themselves because the people had offended God: <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> that notwithstanding this, God was a righteous God, in whom Justice dwelt, and who would be faithful to his Promises.</ns0:note>, even the LORD, the hope of their fathers <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">And he was their hope, and had been he in whom their Fathers before them had hoped, and that not in vain.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 Remove out of the midst of Babylon <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">These words immediately following the other, confirm Mr. <ns0:hi>Calvins</ns0:hi> notion. God by his Prophet commanding his people to remove out of <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> and to go forth chearfully and skipping like the He-goats of the Flock leading the way, and setting an Example unto others. We find much such a call, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 48.20. <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 51.6. which is applied to Spiritual <ns0:hi>Babylon, Rev.</ns0:hi> 18.4. where the coming out is to be understood of a separation from them as to any religious communion, which also was their Duty as to old <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> but that is not the coming out here spoken of.</ns0:note>, and go forth out of the land of the Chaldeans, and be as the he-goats before the flocks.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 ¶ For lo, I will raise and cause to come up against Babylon, an assembly of great nations from the north-country, and they shall set them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves in aray against her <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">He means the <ns0:hi>Medes</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Persian</ns0:hi> (as it is expounded after<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ward)</ns0:note>, from thence she shall be taken: their arrows <ns0:hi>shall be</ns0:hi> as of a mighty <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>destr<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="3 letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•••</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pert man: none shall return in vain <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">I will so direct their arrows, that every arrow they shoot shall pierce one or another. Or, (as some rather chuse to interpret it) no Soldier of that assembly of great Nations, that shall come up against <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> shall return without some Booty or other. The reason of the different reading noted in the Margent, is the difference of a point in the <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> which if set on the right side of the letter, the word signifieth a <ns0:hi>destroyer</ns0:hi>: if on the left side, an <ns0:hi>expert man</ns0:hi> as we translate it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 And Chaldea shall be a spoil: all that spoil her shall be satisfied, saith the LORD <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Satisfied with spoil and plunder, for <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Chaldea</ns0:hi> was at that time one of the richest places in those parts of the world. She was abundant in treasure, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 51.13.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 Because ye were glad, because ye rejoyced <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">They rejoyced at the ruine of the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> the same thing is laid to the charge of the <ns0:hi>Edomites, Obadiah</ns0:hi> 12. The <ns0:hi>Chal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />deans</ns0:hi> were Gods Rod to scourge the <ns0:hi>Iewes,</ns0:hi> but when men are made use of by God, as his Rod and scourge, they ought not to put off Humanity, but to behave themselves decently, and as per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sons that are sensible of the miseries which their brethren suffer.</ns0:note>, O ye destroyers of mine heritage <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">God calls them his heritage, because they formerly were a peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple whom he owned above all other people.</ns0:note>, because ye are grown <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>big<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> corpulent.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> fat, as the heifer at grass, and <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>Neigh as <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                           <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>eeds.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> bellow as bulls <ns0:note n="z" place="margin">There is some difference amongst critical interpreters, whether the heifer here mentioned be to be understood of a heifer at grass (as we tran<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />slate it) or an heifer used to tread out the Corn, or whether it be to be understood of a <ns0:hi>horse-neighing,</ns0:hi> (as the words may be inter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />preted) or an heifer. But these are things of very small mo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment. The cause for which <ns0:hi>Baby<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>on</ns0:hi> is threatned, was doubtless their luxury of all sorts commonly attending great wealth and prosperity meeting with hearts unsanctified.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 Your mother shall be sore confounded, she that bare you shall be ashamed <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Your chief City <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> or your Country, which is the com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mon Mother of all the <ns0:hi>Chaldeans</ns0:hi> shall be destroyed, or shall be ashamed of you, who are not able to defend her.</ns0:note>: behold, the hin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dermost of the nations <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">The sense here seems a little difficult, because it appears no such strange thing that the hindermost of the Nations should be a Wilderness. It is therefore probable that the words <ns0:hi>shall be,</ns0:hi> are to be under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stood before <ns0:hi>the hindermost of the Nations,</ns0:hi> our Translation supplieth them after, so the reading will be <ns0:hi>it shall be the hindermost of the nations, a wilderness,</ns0:hi> &c. That is, <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> that hath been so fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mous, and accounted the head of the Nations, shall become the meanest of all Nations, a meer Wilderness, and a dry land, and a Desert.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>shall be</ns0:hi> a wilderness, a dry land, and a desert.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:62" />13 Because of the wrath of the LORD, it shall not be inhabited, but it shall be wholly desolate <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">The same thing was threatned against <ns0:hi>Babylon, Isa.</ns0:hi> 13.20. <ns0:hi>It shall never be inhabited, neither shall it be dwelt in from generation to generation.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>: every one that goeth by Babylon, shall be astonish<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed, and hiss at all her plagues <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">It seemeth to be a proverbial speech made use of to express the miserable state of a place; we had it before, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 49.17. applyed to <ns0:hi>Edom.</ns0:hi> It is according to the threatning, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 28.37. See <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 25.9, 11. and 29.18. and 42.18. <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 5.15.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 Put your selves in aray against Babylon round about <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">The Prophet calls to the <ns0:hi>Medes</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Persians</ns0:hi> with those who should come with them to their assistance to put themselves in Mi<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>litary order ready to come up against <ns0:hi>Babylon.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>: all ye that bend the bowe, shoot at her, spare no arrows <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">The <ns0:hi>Persians</ns0:hi> (as was noted before) were very famous for the Bow, therefore he speaketh unto them as an Army of Archers, to shoot at the <ns0:hi>Baby<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lonians,</ns0:hi> and to spare no arrows.</ns0:note>: for she hath sinned against the LORD <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Because <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> had sinned a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gainst the Lord exceedingly, as <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 13.13. By their Idolatry, <ns0:hi>Luxury,</ns0:hi> and cruel usage of the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> &c.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 Shout against her round about <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Either as Souldiers use to shout when they fall upon their E<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nemy, or as they use to shout and Triumph when they are entred a City, or when their Enemies fly.</ns0:note>: she hath given her hand <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Either acknowledging them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves overcome, and yielding themselves to the power of their Enemies, or as some think confederating with the <ns0:hi>Lydians,</ns0:hi> but the former is more probable.</ns0:note>: her foundations are faln, her walls are thrown down <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">That is, she is wholly subdued and conquered, as if her Walls were thrown down, for literally her Walls were not beaten down by <ns0:hi>Cyrus,</ns0:hi> for he took the City by surprize.</ns0:note>: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 51.6, 11. Rev. 18.6.</ns0:note> for it <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the venge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ance of the LORD <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">God is he who brings this Vengeance upon <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> though it be by your hands.</ns0:note>: take vengeance upon her; as she hath done, do unto her <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">It is very observable, that there is hardly any sins which the Lord so ordinarily punisheth in the like kind, as those which are offences against the Lawes of <ns0:hi>Iustice</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Charity.</ns0:hi> The common fate of cruel and uncharitable men, is to meet with others to do to them, as they have done to others, unmerciful men find no mercy. See <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 137.8, 9. <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 1.6, 7. <ns0:hi>Adoni-Bezek</ns0:hi> acknowledged Gods Justice in it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 Cut off the sower from Babylon, and him that handleth the <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>Sithe.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> sickle in the time of harvest <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">We are told that <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> was so large a City that within the Walls of it there was much plowed ground: or else the threatning imports that God would deal more severely with <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> than Con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />querors use to do with places which they Conquer, who use to spare and leave behind them. Plow-men, and such as use to Till the ground, but in the destruction of <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> it should not be so.</ns0:note>: for fear of the oppressing sword, they shall turn every one to his people, and they shall flee every one to his own land <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">He speaks either of such strangers as for commerce had their abodes in <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> or such Assistants as the <ns0:hi>Babylonians</ns0:hi> had gotten a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gainst their Enemies, who upon the coming in of the Enemies should make as much haste home as they could.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 ¶ Israel <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> a scattered sheep <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">By <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi> is here meant the whole 12 Tribes (though some<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />times it signifieth the ten Tribes in opposition to <ns0:hi>Iudah</ns0:hi>) they were all wandering sheep, they became penally scattered sheep.</ns0:note>, the lions have driven <ns0:hi>him</ns0:hi> away <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Enemies as fierce and cruel as lions, had seized them, and carried them into Captivity.</ns0:note>, first the king of Assyria hath devoured him <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">First the King of <ns0:hi>Assyria</ns0:hi> de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />voured the Ten Tribes which were strictly call'd, <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> 2 <ns0:hi>Kin.</ns0:hi> 17.6. Then <ns0:hi>Nebuchadnezzar</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>King of Babylon</ns0:hi> took <ns0:hi>Ierusalem</ns0:hi> as we heard <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 39. and carried away the People, and burnt the Temple, which the Prophet here calls a breaking of <ns0:hi>his bones.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, and last this Nebuchadrez<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />zar king of Babylon hath broken his bones.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 Therefore thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, Behold, I will punish the king of Ba<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bylon, and his land <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">God may justly punish those who do the things which he hath commanded them to do, if they do it not in that manner which he directeth, or, if what they do, be not done in obedience to his command, but in satisfaction to their own lusts, which was the case of the <ns0:hi>Assyrians, Isa.</ns0:hi> 10.7.</ns0:note>, as I have punished the king of Assyria <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Some refer this to the punish<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment of the <ns0:hi>Assyrians</ns0:hi> in the destruction of <ns0:hi>Senacherib</ns0:hi> and his Army in the time of <ns0:hi>Hezekiah,</ns0:hi> but the Prophet seemeth here to speak of a destruction of <ns0:hi>Assyria,</ns0:hi> which followed after his devouring of the Ten Tribes, from whence we may conclude, that <ns0:hi>Assyria</ns0:hi> was destroyed before the time of this Revelation.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 And I will bring Israel again to his habitati<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">This must be understood of <ns0:hi>Iudah,</ns0:hi> which was part of that people who were called <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> for to this day we have neither read nor heard of the ten Tribes being brought back again to their habitation.</ns0:note>, and he shall feed on Carmel and Bashan, and his soul shall be satisfied upon mount Ephraim and Gilead <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">The onely difficulty is how it is said that the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> upon their return should feed upon <ns0:hi>Carmel</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Ba<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>han,</ns0:hi> and mount <ns0:hi>Ephraim</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Gilead,</ns0:hi> which were places that belong'd not to the Tribes of <ns0:hi>Iudah</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Benjamin:</ns0:hi> to which it is answered, that these places were granted to the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> by <ns0:hi>Demetrius</ns0:hi> the Father and the Son, as we are told by <ns0:hi>Iosephus, l.</ns0:hi> 13. <ns0:hi>c.</ns0:hi> 5.8. These places were rich Grounds for feeding Cattel, therefore it is said <ns0:hi>they shall feed on Carmel</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Bashan, &c.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 In those dayes, and in that time, saith the LORD, the iniquity of Israel shall be sought for, and <ns0:hi>there shall be</ns0:hi> none: and the sins of Judah, and they shall not be found <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">Some here restrain the term iniquity to <ns0:hi>the idolatry</ns0:hi> of the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> which indeed was their great sin, which God did more especially punish them for, and after the Captivity of <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> we do not read of their offending in that kind, which was according to the Prophesie of <ns0:hi>Isaiah, Isa.</ns0:hi> 27.9. that when God should make the stones of the Altar as Chalk-stones that are beaten asunder, the Groves and the Images should not stand up.</ns0:note>, for I will pardon them whom I reserve <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">But the last words seem to guide us to a larger sense of the term <ns0:hi>iniquity,</ns0:hi> and to point us to another sense of the whole former phrase, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> That God would no longer punish the sins of the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> they should be sought for as to punishment, and not found. And those words <ns0:hi>and none</ns0:hi> must be understood <ns0:hi>as if none,</ns0:hi> they shall be punished no more than if they had none.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">For as to those whom I save from the Captivity of <ns0:hi>Babylon, I will pardon them,</ns0:hi> not that they were all excused from the obligation their sins laid them under as to E<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ternal death, but that their <ns0:hi>Temporal</ns0:hi> punishment was remitted to the whole Body of the <ns0:hi>Iews:</ns0:hi> and those that were truly penitent also, should be discharged from their obligation to Eternal death. The obligation that sin layeth the sinner under to Eternal death may be remitted, and yet the temporal punishment due to them may remain, 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 12.13, 14, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> And on the other side the punishment in this life, may be suspended or remitted, and the obligation, sin layeth the sinner under to Eternal death, may re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />main.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 ¶ Go up against the land of <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>of the Ru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lers,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Rebels.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> Merathaim <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">There is some disputes amongst interpreters whether the words here <ns0:hi>Merathaim</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Pekod</ns0:hi> be to be taken as common nouns, the one signifying <ns0:hi>Rebels</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Rulers,</ns0:hi> the other Visitation, because the <ns0:hi>Chaldeans</ns0:hi> were Rebels against the Lord, and were great Ru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lers over all the contiguous Nations. Or whether they be proper Names of some Places which <ns0:hi>Cyrus</ns0:hi> passed by, or it may be took in, and conquered in his way to <ns0:hi>Babylon.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> against it, and against the inhabitants of <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>Visitation.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> Pe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />kod <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">There is some disputes amongst interpreters whether the words here <ns0:hi>Merathaim</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Pekod</ns0:hi> be to be taken as common nouns, the one signifying <ns0:hi>Rebels</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Rulers,</ns0:hi> the other Visitation, because the <ns0:hi>Chaldeans</ns0:hi> were Rebels against the Lord, and were great Ru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lers over all the contiguous Nations. Or whether they be proper Names of some Places which <ns0:hi>Cyrus</ns0:hi> passed by, or it may be took in, and conquered in his way to <ns0:hi>Babylon.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, waste and utterly destroy after them, saith the LORD, and do according to all that I have commanded thee <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">The latter are Gods words by his Prophet, like the former commanding him with his Armies to go up, and destroy them flying away, or them that should succeed after them, their whole posterity; intimating Gods design utterly to destroy them which destruction was gently be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gun by <ns0:hi>Cyrus,</ns0:hi> and perfected by <ns0:hi>Darius.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22 A sound of battel <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> in the land, and of great destruction <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">That is in the land of <ns0:hi>Caldea.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23 How is the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 51.20.</ns0:note> hammer of the whole earth cut asunder and broken? how is Babylon become a desolation among the nations <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">The latter part of the verse expounds the former, God had made the <ns0:hi>Babylonians</ns0:hi> his Hammer, to break other Nations in pieces, now it was it self broken, the particle <ns0:hi>how</ns0:hi>? may be un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derstood either as expressing triumph and rejoycing, or admira<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion, or as inquiring how such a thing could be in the last sense, the next verse is an answer to this.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">24 I have laid a snare for thee, and thou art also taken, O Babylon, and thou wast not aware, thou art found, and also caught <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">We are told that <ns0:hi>Cyrus</ns0:hi> with his great Army diverted the River <ns0:hi>E<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>phrates</ns0:hi> so as his Army passed over and so surprized the Ci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty so suddenly that those in the midst of it, did not know it when part of the City was already taken. God directed <ns0:hi>Cyrus</ns0:hi> to this Stratagem for the taking of the City, which the Prophet calls a <ns0:hi>snar<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>,</ns0:hi> wherein the <ns0:hi>Babylonians</ns0:hi> were taken when</ns0:note>, because thou hast stri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ven against the LORD <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">the reason of this unexpected ruine to this great people was their sin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ning against the Lord <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 14. which is here call'd a <ns0:hi>striving</ns0:hi> a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gainst him, as indeed all sin is.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:63" />25 The LORD hath opened his armoury, and hath brought forth the weapons of his indignati<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on: for this <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the work of the LORD God of hosts, in the land of the Chaldeans <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> was so rich, and potent a Nation, and had been so great a conquerour that people looking onely with the eye of sense, and judging according to probabilities in the eyes of men, might well ask how these things could possibly be? to which the Prophet here answereth. That the hand of God was to be eyed in the case, this was the Lords work upon the <ns0:hi>Chaldeans</ns0:hi>; God had opened his Armoury, and the <ns0:hi>Medes</ns0:hi> were to make use of the weapons of his indignation. He who threatned this destruction was able to carry it through, and it was no great matter what weapons either the <ns0:hi>Babylonians</ns0:hi> had to defend themselves, or the <ns0:hi>Medes</ns0:hi> to offend them, it was Gods power and strength was onely to be regarded.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="26">26 Come against her <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>from the end.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> from the utmost bor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">The Prophet in the name of God calleth to the Enemies of <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Medes,</ns0:hi> to come up, from the furthest parts of their dominions, or from all parts, to fight against <ns0:hi>Babylon.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, open her store-houses <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">To open the Granaries, or Storehouses or Treasuries of the <ns0:hi>Babylonians.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>: <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>tread her.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> cast her up as heaps <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">And to cast up the Cities as <ns0:hi>heaps</ns0:hi> of Rubbish, and utterly to de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stroy the City with such a total destruction that nothing of it should be left.</ns0:note>, and destroy her utterly: let nothing of her be left.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="27">27 Slay all her bullocks: let them go down to the slaughter <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">By Bullocks in this place Interpreters generally understand the great and rich men of <ns0:hi>Babylon.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>: wo unto them, for their day is come, the time of their visitation.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="28">28 The voice of them that flee and escape out of the land of Babylon <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 51.10, 11.</ns0:note> to declare in Zion the ven<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />geance of the LORD our God, the vengeance of his temple <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">The Prophet here, brings in the poor <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> that had been Captives in <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> going back upon <ns0:hi>Cyrus</ns0:hi> his Proclamation of Liberty, towards <ns0:hi>Zion</ns0:hi> there joyfully to declare the Revenge which their God had taken for them, and for his Holy <ns0:hi>Temple,</ns0:hi> which the <ns0:hi>Chaldeans</ns0:hi> had burnt and destroyed.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="29">29 Call together the archers against Babylon <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">The word translated <ns0:hi>Archers</ns0:hi> signifieth also <ns0:hi>many,</ns0:hi> and is by di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vers so translated, but the following words more justifie our tran<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />slation.</ns0:note>: all ye that bend the bowe, camp against it round about; let none thereof escape, recompense her according to her work; according to all that she hath done, do unto her: for she hath been proud against the LORD, against the holy One of Israel <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">The cause of Gods calling for <ns0:hi>Babylons</ns0:hi> Enemies against her, is assigned to be her Pride against the Lord.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="30">30 Therefore shall her young men fall in the streets, and all her men of war shall be cut off in that day <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">See <ns0:hi>Chapter</ns0:hi> 49.26. where we met with the same words.</ns0:note>, saith the LORD.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="31">31 Behold, I <ns0:hi>am</ns0:hi> against thee, O <ns0:hi>thou</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>Pride.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> most proud, saith the LORD God of hosts, for thy day is come, the time <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> I will visit thee <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> is particularly branded for Pride, which is the swel<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ling of a mans heart in a self opinion, caused from some thing wherein he excelleth, or thinks that he excelleth another. We have a large account of the Pride of <ns0:hi>Babylon, Isa.</ns0:hi> 14.12, 13, 14. and particularly of one of their Kings, <ns0:hi>Dan.</ns0:hi> 5.20, 21. The sin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ner exalteth himself against God, and either judgeth himself wiser, or more mighty than he.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="32">32 And the <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>Pride.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> most proud shall stumble and fall, and none shall raise him up: and I will kindle a fire in his cities, and it shall devour all round a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bout him <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> before called <ns0:hi>the most Proud,</ns0:hi> here <ns0:hi>Pride</ns0:hi> in the abstract (which speaketh this people excessively faulty in this thing) shall fall, and so fall, as never more to be recovered and raised up.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="33">¶ 33 Thus saith the LORD of hosts, The chil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dren of Israel and the children of Judah <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> op<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pressed together <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Not together in respect of times, for there was 150 years dif<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ference betwixt the time of <ns0:hi>Israels</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Iudahs</ns0:hi> captivity, nor by the same Enemy <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi> was carried away Captive by the <ns0:hi>Assyrians, Iudah,</ns0:hi> by the <ns0:hi>Caldeans. Together</ns0:hi> in this place signifies no more than that they were both oppressed, or alike oppressed.</ns0:note>, and all that took them cap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tives held them fast, they refused to let them go <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">And some may think that my Prophesies are but Flatteries, and vain words, for those who have them in their hands are able to keep them, and will not be willing to let them go.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="34">34 Their redeemer <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> strong, the LORD of hosts <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> his name <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">The Lord whose name is the Lord of Hosts, is he that is their Avenger: (for so the word signifies, and he is as strong as any of those that hold them fast, and will not let them go.</ns0:note>, he shall throughly plead their cause <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">He will plead their cause, not like a Lawyer, but actually, and really effect it, as pleading is often taken, as <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 25.31. <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 17.20. <ns0:hi>Ioel</ns0:hi> 3.2.</ns0:note>, that he may give rest to the land, and dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quiet the inhabitants of Babylon <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">These are the two ends which God aimeth at, to give his peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple rest, and to punish <ns0:hi>Babylon.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="35">35 ¶ A sword <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">That is, there shall come a sword, the sword of the <ns0:hi>Medes,</ns0:hi> upon <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> and all the Land of the <ns0:hi>Chaldeans,</ns0:hi> and all orders of Persons in it.</ns0:note> upon the Chaldeans, saith the LORD, and upon the inhabitants of Baby<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lon, and upon her princes, and upon her wise <ns0:hi>men.</ns0:hi>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="36">36 A sword <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> upon the <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>chief <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                     </ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> liars, and they shall dote <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">The word here translated Liars, is by some translated <ns0:hi>barrs,</ns0:hi> by some <ns0:hi>liars</ns0:hi>; and in the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> it hath both significations; which makes some think it is to be understood of the chief men who are the Props, Stays and Bars of a place whose Wisdom God threatens should fail them, so as they should dote, and shew themselves Fools. Others Translating it <ns0:hi>liars</ns0:hi> as we do, understand it of their Soothsayers and Wizzards whom he calls <ns0:hi>liars,</ns0:hi> because they divined false, and saith they should dote, not foreseeing what should be.</ns0:note>: a sword <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> upon her mighty men, and they shall be dismayed <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">And though they were full of valiant mighty men, yet, their hearts should fail them when this day came, and all be destroyed amongst the rest.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="37">37 A sword <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> upon their horses, and upon their chariots <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Though they be full of Chariots and Horses, the Enemy shall destroy them.</ns0:note>, and upon all the mingled people that <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> in the midst of her <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">By the mingled people some understand those whom the <ns0:hi>Babylonians</ns0:hi> had hired to their Assistance from other Nations, others, such strangers as lived amongst them; others a people under the power of the <ns0:hi>Chaldeans,</ns0:hi> made up of People of several Countries. See <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 25.20, 24. <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 30.5. they seem to signifie a people that were not Native <ns0:hi>Caldeans</ns0:hi> but under their dominion.</ns0:note>, and they shall become <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Nah. 3.13. Isa. 13.15. chap. 46.<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> as women <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">That is, faint-hearted.</ns0:note>, a sword <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> upon her treasures, and they shall be robbed <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">And though <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> hath great Treasures, yet those shall not secure her, she shall be robbed of them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="38">38 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 51.3<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 36.</ns0:note> A drought <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> upon her waters, and they shall be dried up <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Some think that this phrase hath a special reference to <ns0:hi>Cyrus</ns0:hi> his Stratagem used in the surprize of <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> one part of it was fortified by the great River <ns0:hi>Euphrates,</ns0:hi> running on one side, which <ns0:hi>Cyrus</ns0:hi> diverted by cutting several Channels, till he had drained it so low, that it became passable for his Army to go over: Others think that a want of Rain is here threatned.</ns0:note>, for it <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the land of graven ima<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ges, and they are mad upon <ns0:hi>their</ns0:hi> idols <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">God gives the reason of this Judgment which was their Idolatry, and exceeding zeal for it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="39">39 Therefore <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 13.22. & 34.14. chap. 51 37. Rev. 18.2.</ns0:note> the wilde beasts of the deserts with the wilde beasts of the islands shall dwell <ns0:hi>there,</ns0:hi> and the owls shall dwell therein: and it shall be no more inhabited for ever: neither shall it be dwelt in from generation to generation.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="40">40 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gen<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 19.2<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. Isa. 13.19. chap. 49.18.</ns0:note> As God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and the neighbour <ns0:hi>cities</ns0:hi> thereof, saith the LORD: <ns0:hi>so</ns0:hi> shall no man abide there <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">The substance of both these verses is, that <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> should be totally ruined, as <ns0:hi>Sodom</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Gomorrah</ns0:hi> so as there should be no Habitations for men, but wild beasts onely of all sorts should inha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bit and lodge in it. The fulfilling of this we have not in holy Writ, only the beginning of its accomplishment, it being taken by <ns0:hi>Cyrus</ns0:hi> who only made them Tributaries, and took away their Government. But they rebelling against the <ns0:hi>Emperour</ns0:hi> of the <ns0:hi>Medes, Dari<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>s Hystaspis</ns0:hi> a succeeding Emperour pulled down their walls. And about 250 years after <ns0:hi>Seleucus Nicanor</ns0:hi> a Grecian Prince the <ns0:hi>Medes</ns0:hi> being before conquered by <ns0:hi>Alexander the Great,</ns0:hi> utterly destroyed <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> so as in the time of <ns0:hi>Hadri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />an</ns0:hi> the Roman Emperour, there was nothing left standing of that great City but some pieces of walls.</ns0:note>, neither shall any son of man dwell therein.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="41">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:63" />41 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 6.22.</ns0:note> Behold, a people shall come from the north, and a great nation, and many kings shall be raised up from the coasts of the earth <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">The <ns0:hi>Medes</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Persians</ns0:hi> with their Armies, who shall also have many other Kings, who from the several parts of the earth shall join with him and help him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="42">42 They shall hold the bow and the lance <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">These were the two usual weapons of Souldiers in those Countries, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 6.23.</ns0:note>: they <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> cruel and will not shew mercy <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">The <ns0:hi>Persians</ns0:hi> were a cruel bloody people.</ns0:note>: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 5.30.</ns0:note> their voice shall roar like the seas, and they shall ride up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on horses, <ns0:hi>every one</ns0:hi> put in array like a man to the battel, against thee, O daughter of Babylon <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">These phrases signifie no more, then that the Enemies should come upon <ns0:hi>Babylon</ns0:hi> in a terrible manner, and prepared to destroy them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="43">43 The king of Babylon hath heard the report of them, and his hands waxed feeble: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 49.24.</ns0:note> anguish took hold on him, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> pangs as of a woman in travail <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">The <ns0:hi>Medes</ns0:hi> shall not be more prepared to destroy the <ns0:hi>Baby<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lonians,</ns0:hi> then they shall be unprepared to make any resistance, as God will animate their Enemies, so he will dispirit them, so as they shall faint upon the report of their coming, and be like a woman upon whom strong pangs of travail are.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="44">44 Behold, he shall come up <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Job 41.10.</ns0:note> like a lion from the swelling of Jordan, unto the habitation of the strong: but I will make them suddenly run away from her: and who <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> a chosen <ns0:hi>man that</ns0:hi> I may appoint over her? for who <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> like me? and who will <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>convent me to plead.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> appoint me the time? and who <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> that shepherd that will stand before me?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="45">45 Therefore hear ye the counsel of the LORD, that he hath taken against Babylon, and his pur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />poses that he hath purposed against the land of the Caldeans: surely the least of the flock shall draw them out: surely he shall make <ns0:hi>their</ns0:hi> habita<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion desolate with them <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">See the notes on <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 49.19. where we have applied unto <ns0:hi>Edom</ns0:hi> all that is here spoken against <ns0:hi>Babylon.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="46">46 At the noise of the taking of Babylon the earth is moved, and the cry is heard among the nations <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">We have much the same spoken with reference to <ns0:hi>Edom,</ns0:hi> 49.20. The words are only expressive of the greatness of the destruction of <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> which should be such as should make all that part of the World shake, and the noise of it would ring throughout all the Nations in that part of the Earth.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
            </ns0:div>
